en: Preface to the *Direct Pointing to the West* (*Xifang Zhizhi*).
This *Direct Pointing to the West* was composed by the lay practitioner Lütian Yinian. Its intent is to inform those who have not yet heard of the Western [Pure Land].
The work fully elucidates the phenomena and characteristics [of the Pure Land] without departing from the nature and mind; thus, readers believe in it.
If one understands this teaching and puts it into practice, will it not only evoke the Western Pure Land, but also manifest the *Sāmbhogika* (Jigaku) Pure Land?
Therefore, I have now brought it forth from among the archives of our own mountain monastery and commissioned carvers to engrave it for wide dissemination;
it is my humble hope that this work may endure forever, remaining imperishable.
Preface to the *Western Direct Pointing*,
recorded by the Śramaṇa Dayun (Liangrun) of Mount Tiantai on the first day of the eighth month of the year Xinwei of the Genroku era at the Xiyue Temple on East Creek.

The Layman Yuan composed the *Western Pure Land Synthesis* (*Xi-fang he-lun*) to inform those who have not yet attained awakening through Chan meditation, while I, in turn, composed the *Direct Pointing to the West* (*Xi-fang zhi-zhi*) to inform those who have not heard of the Western Pure Land.
Someone said, "You are a follower of Confucianism; can you take Chan as your school?
I replied, "I am one who rejects Chan; I do not take Chan as my school. For Chan and Confucianism each establish their own gateways, and originally there is no connection between them."
Since the teachings of the world have not been clarified, people have given rise to thorns of sectarian views;
thus, there are those who exclude Chan, those who favor Chan, those who synthesize Confucianism and Chan, and those who analyze Confucianism and Chan.

Their debates are manifold and lack any firm foundation, causing wicked scholars and mad followers to take advantage of the situation to engage in fraud and hide within these ranks. This not only brings discredit upon Confucianism, but also brings discredit upon Chan. However...
Therefore, those who wish to open up a path for Chan should not merely dispute its name, but rather attack its maladies.
This shall cause practitioners of Chan to understand how it truly begins as Chan, so that they do not allow the maladies of Chan to afflict Chan itself;

and it shall cause practitioners of Confucianism to understand that such [maladies] are not even Chan, so that they do not allow the maladies of Chan to afflict Confucianism—just as one who eats grain does not sow wheat.
Because one can recognize wheat, one does not hear of anyone rejecting wheat, yet in the end one does not consider wheat superior to grain; those who eat wheat do not plant grain.
Likewise, because one can recognize grain, one does not hear of anyone rejecting grain, yet in the end one does not consider grain superior to wheat.
This is for no other reason than that when comparing grain and wheat, it is like comparing black and white—there is no room for rejection, and in truth, rejection is unnecessary. Thus it is.
Therefore, when Confucius praised Laozi as "old yet not old," it was because Confucius was able to know Laozi;
when Hanzi refuted Buddhism yet yielded to it, it was because Hanzi did not know Buddhism.
Now, to attack something without knowing its ailment, merely refuting it from its own gateway—not only will the Chan practitioners resist it, but even the Confucians will be suspicious of it.
Since even those who refute Chan have themselves harbored doubts, it is better to confront them openly than to harbor suspicions in secret.
If one can distinguish between them clearly, then Chan will not obstruct Confucianism, and Confucianism will not obstruct Chan; why then trouble oneself with polemical refutations? Someone might say:

"Nowadays, the poison of Chan has spread widely, infecting our own Confucian tradition. If you do not defend Confucianism, you are directly attacking the very nest of Chan. This is truly urgent; we must treat the symptoms."

"This is indeed a marvelous strategy. However, in the Chan school, all things are empty and both purity and defilement are forgotten; now you are biasedly attached to the Western Paradise—is this not contrary to principle?
I replied: "Sentient beings mistakenly misinterpret the Patriarch’s intent; their primary ailment is precisely this very view.

Yet you still persist in taking this ailment as the medicine—is this not to be doubly lost within delusion? You must know that for a Chan practitioner, there is the Chan of the Pure Land, and the Pure Land of Chan."
"Earth" refers to the Pure Land of Dhyāna; originally, there are no such manifold conceptualizations or views.

My son, if you cannot see the moon and forget the finger that points to it, then to say the Western Land exists is not the Western Land; to say the Western Land does not exist is not the Western Land;
to say the Western Land both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist, is likewise not the Western Land. To say... [is likewise not the Western Land].
"Meditation is itself the Pure Land, and the Pure Land is itself meditation; both are ultimately mere conceptual proliferations—what, then, do they mean to you?
Nevertheless, practicing other paths is like an ant climbing a high mountain, whereas rebirth through the recitation of the Buddha's name is like a wind-blown sail unfurled upon a following current.
Since the sages have spoken of this with such earnest repetition, what need is there to wait for the dull-witted to realize it?"

Compiled by the Layman Lütian:
The Sutra on the Grounds for Rebirth in the Pure Land states that in the distant past, eons ago, there was a king named Kauśika. At that time, there was a Buddha named...
The Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja heard the Dharma, relinquished his throne, and left the household life, becoming known as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
Before that Buddha, he made forty-eight vows. Among them was one vow which said:

"When I become a Buddha, if sentient beings of the ten directions, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land, and yet do not attain birth by reciting my name ten times—if they do not so attain birth, may I not become a Buddha."
The Buddha, having diligently practiced throughout kalpas, attained Perfect Enlightenment and was named Amitābha; his land is called the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
From here, passing through ten trillion Buddha-fields to the west, he currently resides and preaches the Dharma.

The two great Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, assist him in spreading the transformation. In the Sanskrit language, Amitābha means "Immeasurable," referring to the Buddha's radiance.

Because it illuminates the lands of the ten directions immeasurably, and because both the Buddha’s lifespan and that of its inhabitants endure for immeasurable kalpas, the ground of that land is made of gold.
It is adorned with various features such as no hills, valleys, pits, or hollows, but with jeweled ponds and jeweled trees.
Water-birds, winds, and forests all proclaim the wondrous Dharma together. There is no distinction between day and night, nor cold and heat; there are no hells, hungry ghosts, or animals.
There are women whose clothing, food, drink, and utensils arrive according to their thoughts, and who experience no suffering but only various joys;
therefore, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī), also known as "Peaceful Nurturing" (An-yang), "Pure Tranquility" (Qing-tai), and "Pure Land" (Jingtu).
The *Sutra on the Meritorious Effects of the Pure Land* states:
"Those who wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss should cultivate the three types of merit.

First, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, maintaining a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten virtuous deeds. Second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges and fully observing the various precepts."

Not violating the three aspects of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*)—namely, generating the bodhicitta, having deep faith in cause and effect, and reciting the Mahāyāna while exhorting others to practice—these three matters are called the true cause and root of pure karma. When the roots are mature, one maintains them in their entirety;

when the roots have just arisen, one receives them partially. Furthermore, it is said that if there are those who, with deep faith and aspiration, bring to mind Amitābha Buddha, such persons will, in the present life...

In this world, those who eliminate calamities and increase their lifespan shall have lotus flowers arise within the Western Pool of Seven Jewels; their names shall be inscribed upon them from the moment of conception.

Through single-minded devotion to the Buddha, the flowers will bloom and flourish daily. At the time of death, the Buddha, not forsaking his power of vows, will personally descend to receive and guide them.
Their minds will remain undisturbed, and in a single kṣaṇa, they will go to be born by transformation within the womb of a lotus, according to their purity.
According to the depth of one's karma—whether superior, middling, or inferior—there are nine grades who all attain the vision of the Buddha and hearing of the Dharma;
with minds free from regression, they realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and shall never again transmigrate.
*The Ritual for the Pure Land*
Every morning at dawn, after the practitioner has dressed and refrained from consuming meat or alcohol, they shall burn incense to make offerings to the Buddha.

Setting aside all distracting thoughts, they should focus their minds with single-minded devotion, as if facing the golden countenance of the Buddha, like a child yearning for its mother, or like one trapped in fire or water or in prison seeking rescue.
Having finished prostrating toward the west with palms joined, they should then recite: "Namo Amitābha Buddha."
Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Namo all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and other supreme virtuous ones.
(Recite each name ten times, with each utterance performed in a single breath, neither too high nor too low.
Having finished the recitation, further recite the Verse of Aspiration for Great Compassion once: "Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time..."

The Buddha Amitābha, foremost among all, delivers sentient beings through nine grades of rebirth; his majestic virtue is infinite and boundless. I now take great refuge and repent for the sins of my three karmas.
Whatever merits and virtues exist, I dedicate them with a sincere heart. May the response appear at all times for those who recite the Buddha’s name together with me.
At the moment of death, may the realm of the Western Land be clearly manifest before one's eyes; may all that is seen and heard be pure and sublime.

Furthermore, those whose bodies and minds have some leisure should take as their primary practice the recitation of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Nianfo Wangsheng Zhou* (Recitation of the Mantra for Rebirth), and the *Western Pure Land Vow Text*.

As for other practices, whether performed at two or three sessions of the day, one may recite the Buddha’s name a thousand or ten thousand times. Upon completing these, one should prostrate and withdraw. Having thus resolved to see the Buddha and bring an end to birth and death, and to deliver all beings as the Buddha does, one should then pay homage and retire.
Practice according to your capacity, establishing a fixed routine every day that must not be interrupted for even a single day.
*Pure Land Vow Text* (composed by Chen Lianchi) I bow my head to the Western Land of Peace and Bliss,
To the Great Teacher who receives and guides all sentient beings.
I now make this vow, wishing to be reborn there; may you, out of your compassion, graciously accept me— this disciple (so-and-so and the assembly)—
and for the sake of all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm of the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence,

single-mindedly uphold and recite the vast and majestic name of Amitābha Buddha, endowed with ten thousand virtues, in order to seek the unsurpassed Bodhi of the One Vehicle of all Buddhas, aspiring to be born therein.

Furthermore, in the Pure Land, because our karma is heavy and merit is slight, our hindrances are deep and wisdom is shallow; thus, defiled minds easily flare up while pure virtues are difficult to accomplish.
Now, before the Buddha, we lift our bodies in prostration with diligence, pouring forth our hearts with single-minded sincerity to repent:

from beginningless kalpas until now, both I and all sentient beings have been deluded regarding our inherently pure mind, indulging in greed, anger, and ignorance to defile the three karmas in measureless and boundless ways.
May all the immeasurable and boundless defilements of the sins I have committed, and the karmic enmities I have bound, be entirely extinguished.

From this day forth, I establish a profound vow to distance myself from unwholesome dharmas and vow never to create them again; I vow to diligently cultivate the Noble Path without falling into indolence;
I vow to attain Perfect Enlightenment; and I vow to deliver all sentient beings. May Amitābha Buddha, through the power of his compassionate vows, bear witness to this.
May I be moved by compassion; may I be graced by [the Buddha’s] power. May I, within my meditative contemplation and during my dreams, behold the golden body of Amitābha Buddha;
may I traverse the jewel-adorned lands of Amitābha Buddha; may I receive the nectar-consecration of Amitābha Buddha;
may his light illuminate my body and his hand stroke my head, while his robe covers my form.
May my long-standing obstacles be spontaneously removed and my roots of goodness increase;

may afflictions be swiftly emptied and ignorance suddenly shattered, so that the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment may open up in vast clarity, and the true realm of tranquil light may be constantly manifest before me.

Furthermore, when the time approaches for the end of life, may I know in advance that the moment has come; may my body be free from all illness, suffering, and calamities, and may my mind be free from all attachment and delusion.
Their faculties are joyful and serene, their right mindfulness is clear and distinct, and they experience a tranquil equanimity as if entering meditative absorption.
Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of holy sages, emit light to welcome and guide them, extending their hands to support and lead them.

Celestial palaces, banners, pennants, extraordinary fragrances, and heavenly music manifest the sacred realm of the West before their very eyes, so that all sentient beings who see or hear it may be transformed.
Filled with joy and moved by deep admiration, I resolved to attain Bodhicitta.

At that time, riding upon a vajra pedestal and following behind the Buddha, in the mere twinkling of an eye, I was born within a lotus flower made of the seven treasures in a pool of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

There, amidst the blossoming lotus, I beheld the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas, heard the wondrous sound of the Dharma, and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). In an instant, I attended upon all the [buddhas].

The Buddha personally bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon him; having received this prediction, he fully accomplished all merits, including the three bodies, the four wisdoms, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharani-gates.

Thereafter, without departing from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), he returned to the Sahā world, manifesting countless emanations throughout the lands of the ten directions by means of inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers.

By means of various skillful expedients, may I deliver all sentient beings, causing them all to leave defilement behind, regain their pure minds, be reborn together in the Western Land, and enter the stage of non-retrogression.

Such great vows are inexhaustible; as long as the world is inexhaustible, sentient beings are inexhaustible, and karma and afflictions are entirely inexhaustible, so too shall my vows be inexhaustible.
I now pay homage to the Buddha, make this vow, and dedicate the merit of my practice for the benefit of others.

Repaying the four debts of gratitude to sentient beings throughout the three realms of existence, providing universal sustenance so that all beings within the Dharma-realm may together perfect the All-Knowing Wisdom;
a selection of clarifications regarding Pure Lands and the direct pointing to the source.
Zongben asked his disciples, "I wish to escape birth and death, yet I do not know upon what dharma I should rely for cultivation.
The Chan Master praised him, saying, "Your age is young, yet your resolve is lofty. Listen to what I say regarding the direct path of cultivation: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Zongben said, "Ordinary people have vast karmic offenses; how can one attain rebirth there merely by reciting the Buddha's name for a single lifetime?"
[They] will be born in the Pure Land. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra in Sixteen Contemplations* states:
"A single utterance of 'Namo Amitābha Buddha' with a sincere mind extinguishes the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

If someone who has committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds throughout their life can still attain rebirth by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times at the moment of death, how much more so for one who observes the precepts and recites the Buddha's name throughout an entire lifetime?"
Question: For what reason does Amitābha Buddha possess such vast merit, vast practices, and vast vows?
Answer: The *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* states: "When I attain Buddhahood, my name and fame shall transcend the ten directions;

humans and devas shall joyfully hear it and all come to be born in my land; even those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals shall likewise be born within my land. Thus, for all who are...
It can be known that there is nothing within the cycle of the three realms and six paths that he does not deliver.

Amitābha Buddha currently resides in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, yet he also teaches and transforms countless devas and humans throughout the worlds of the ten directions, even down to the classes of creatures that fly and wriggle (those that "fly" refers to minute insects; those that "wriggle" refers to minute larvae). Such is his reach.
If even the Buddhas transform and deliver others, how much more so should humans? Furthermore, Amitābha Buddha made this vow:
"If one calls upon my name, they shall surely be born in my land; if it were otherwise, I would not attain Buddhahood.

For this reason, he delivers sentient beings extensively without end, and yet by relying on him for even a single thought-moment, one is born in his land. From this, one can infer the merit of reciting the Buddha's name.

This is truly inconceivable. Furthermore, it is said that if there are sentient beings who wish to be born in my land in the highest grade, they must employ a heart of compassion, refrain from killing, and cherish all living beings;

they must possess all the precepts, read and recite the Mahāyāna, understand the principle of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), deeply clarify its meaning, make offerings to the Triple Gem, show filial piety to their parents, take pity on the poor and suffering, and transform those who have not yet been transformed.
If one can practice mindfulness of the Buddha with such sincerity, one will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest level and proceed directly to Buddhahood.

Should one’s strength be insufficient, however, if they maintain the fasts and precepts and practice mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded devotion, and if their mindfulness of the Buddha is uninterrupted, they will at least not be born in the lowest grade.
Moreover, this Dharma gate makes no distinction between the worthy and the foolish, nor does it choose between the noble and the lowly.
Regardless of wealth or poverty, male or female, old or young, monastic or lay, or the length of time one has practiced, all may recite the Buddha’s name.

Furthermore, the method of recitation is unrestricted: one may recite aloud, recite in a low voice, recite like a flowing stream, recite while prostrating, recite through investigation, recite with visualization, recite with focused concentration, recite while turning a prayer bead rosary, recite while walking, or recite while standing still.

Establish mindfulness while sitting, mindfulness while lying on one’s side, silent mindfulness, and clear mindfulness—whether a thousand thoughts or ten thousand thoughts, they are all but a single thought.
It is essential only to possess resolute faith and seek birth in the Pure Land. If one can practice in this way, what need is there to seek out other teachers?
It may be said that the entire art of rowing a boat lies with the helmsman; those who attain this realization shall together ascend to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Question:
People of the world often say that they are entangled by family affairs and bound by worldly duties, and thus must wait until old age before they can practice the Buddha-recitation.
The answer is: "How bitter! How bitter! Have you not seen what Chan Master Sīxin said?

'People of the world have wealth and treasures as high as mountains and wives and concubines filling their rooms; they enjoy themselves day and night. Do they not also desire to live long in this world?'"
Alas, how can one resist the limits of the future life, which secretly hasten us on? When the summons arrives, we must depart; there is no room for delay.
The Old Man of Yama does not accommodate human sentiment; what face would the King of Impermanence have?

Relying on what you yourselves have personally seen with your eyes and heard with your ears—those close relatives, kinsmen, friends, and brothers, once so strong, now gone from the streets and alleys before and behind.
How much more will there be of birth and death hereafter? Have you not heard the ancients say: "Do not wait until old age to study the Way;

the solitary graves are all but young men"? And they also said: "Since early years one seeks a wife and raises children, managing the household affairs and undergoing a thousand hardships and ten thousand sufferings;
yet when the three-inch breath suddenly ceases, one cannot avoid having everything come to rest in a single day. If this is so...
Filial sons and grandsons together obtain a portion of the monastic community; they read a section of the scriptures and burn bundles of paper money.
In the third month of spring and the ninth month of autumn, they prepare bowls of rice and wail until the trees themselves cry out. This is still merely remembering one's parents.
If, however, there are unfilial children whose parents have only just died while their bones are still warm, they seize the property, sell the fields and gardens, and act as they please.
If one compares this with that, what urgency is there? Grandchildren have their own blessings; do not serve as a horse or an ox for them.
Again, citing an ancient worthy, he said: With a cold laugh, I look upon the wealthy householder: His livelihood is as frantic as a speeding arrow. The granaries are full, yet the rice breeds worms;
The storehouses are filled, yet the coins rot in bundles. By day he weighs out straw; By night he lights lamps to calculate his wealth— All for the sake of this physical frame.
Like a puppet, do not let the strings snap; with such bitter words I have exhorted you:
"I once promised you that you might attend to worldly affairs until old age, and then practice the Buddha's name. You should reflect: how much time can a person have in this world?
Like sparks from a flint or a flash of lightning, it passes in the blink of an eye. Seize this time before you are old and before you are ill, and shake yourself free—both body and mind.
Cast aside worldly affairs to seize a single day’s light; recite the Buddha’s name for a single day and devote a single period of time to cultivating pure karma.
Whether one meets a good death or a bad death at the end of life depends on this:
my provisions have been prepared in advance, and my future path is secure and certain. If it is not so, what can be done to remedy regret later?
Reflect upon it, reflect upon it!
An excerpt from the *Ten Doubts Treatise* by the Tiantai Master Zhiyi:
"Pointing to the Ultimate Goal of the Pure Land."
Is it perhaps considered difficult in this world for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha to attain rebirth?
If even the most ignorant men and women can uphold the sacred name with sincere faith and without doubt, there are none who will not attain rebirth. Or is it perhaps considered easy?

Were it not for those who have planted deep roots in past lives, who penetrate the profound mysteries, and who are not hindered by partial or inferior views, they would be unable to perceive its essential core and fundamental principle.

The Sūtra states that those who cultivate goodness with a doubting mind fail to comprehend the Buddha’s wisdom and are born in that womb-palace for five hundred years, where they do not see the Triple Gem;
yet the causes for such a superior rebirth are truly a waste, as they fail to understand the primary meaning.
Thus we know that clarifying the fundamental principle and attaining its essence is the precursor to all practices; how can those who cultivate pure karma afford to be negligent?

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Scripture on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha) states: "The Tathāgata now teaches Vaidehī and all sentient beings of future ages to contemplate the Western World of Ultimate Bliss;
by the power of the Buddha, they shall behold that pure land."

By purifying the buddha-field— just as one sees the reflection of one's own face by holding a bright mirror— and by seeing the supremely wondrous and blissful matters of that land with a heart of joy,
one immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at that very moment.

Regarding "the three contemplations within one mind," the Venerable Master of the Four Clarities said: "The three contemplations mean that in a single thought-moment, it is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way. What is called 'empty' means that all things are empty;
this is the function of the three contemplations manifesting to sweep away the appearance of substantiality. What is called 'provisionally existent' means that all things are provisional."

The three contemplations are all clear in their function of establishing dharmas; that which is "central" is such that all things are central, and the three contemplations are all the absolute, non-referential essence.
Thus, though one spends all day dispelling characteristics, all dharmas are fully realized; though one spends all day establishing dharmas, not even a speck of dust remains;
though one spends all day transcending relativity, the two truths blaze forth. This is the inconceivable marvel.
It is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Taking the contemplation of the mind as its core principle,
the Venerable Zongxing of Siming’s *Miaozongchao* (Commentary on the *Miaozong*) explains that while the Sutra takes "contemplating the Buddha" as its title, the present commentary [now]...
Taking the contemplation of the mind as the primary principle, these two [approaches] are fundamentally no different; this is precisely what constitutes the present contemplation.

It is because the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) is entirely distinct from the Lesser Vehicle—that the Lesser Vehicle is dimly aware only of the "mind-only" while perceiving the Buddha as existing externally. Practitioners of the Mahayana know that their own single mind is replete with the Buddha-nature;

by relying on external objects to cultivate contemplation, the marks of the Buddha then become manifest. In the present contemplation, the Buddha Amitābha’s environment and his physical body serve as conditions to permeate the mind.

The nature of mind and that which is possessed by the mind—the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, both its environment and its inhabitants—arise through the power of perfuming from what is possessed by the mind.
How could they ever be separate from the nature of mind? The entire mind is Buddha, and the entire Buddha is mind. To contemplate the mind all day is to contemplate the Buddha all day.
Therefore, although the wording of the Sūtra and the Commentary differs, their meaning is no different. Furthermore, one must understand that whoever contemplates the Buddha [necessarily...]

One must illumine the mind. If one contemplates the mind exclusively, it is not necessarily a case of relying upon the Buddha as the object of focus, such as in the *Ekakṣaṇa-samādhi*, where one directly contemplates a single thought-moment without relying on another Buddha as the focal point.
However, in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* and this method of contemplation, one begins by contemplating the Pure Land and its inhabitants (the environment and the beings therein).
Because these environments and beings are not separate from the nature of the mind, it is called "contemplation of the mind. One must understand this contemplation.

One does not focus exclusively on observing the mind, but divides it into internal and external aspects; this present practice constitutes external observation because it relies upon the contemplation of that [Buddha] as both the support (the environment) and the supported (the Buddha-body).
For this reason, the title of the sutra is called "Contemplating the Buddha. Regarding the difficulty or ease of the practice, one must now follow the easier method.

The *Fahua Xuanzan* states: "The Buddha-dharma is exceedingly lofty and sentient beings are exceedingly vast; for a beginner, this is difficult. However, when mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are seen as the three non-differentiated realities, [the path becomes easy]."
Contemplating the mind is easy; this present method of contemplation does not merely involve contemplating the Buddha, but rather relies on the contemplation of the mind.

By taking the lower to manifest the high, even though one practices the contemplation of the Buddha, it is not called difficult. Thus we know that the central tenet of this sutra is the contemplation of the mind, and because the intent is to see the Buddha through this, two modes of explanation are obtained.
Their meanings do not follow divergent paths. Furthermore, one should know that the inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused *dharmadhātu* acts as [the basis for these].
A single thought-moment of my mind likewise manifests its entire substance as birth, as the Buddha, as the support, as the correct, as the root, and as the object;
from a single mind to a single speck of dust, down to a single atom, there is nothing that does not manifest as the entire Dharma-realm.

Since each and every phenomenon manifests as the entire Dharma-realm, to raise up any one of them is precisely the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm in its full extent. Since it is fully present, it is the Dharma-realm.
Within the realms (*dhātu*), what single thing is not endowed with all phenomena (*dharma*), since each and every phenomenon is endowed with all phenomena?
This is the general and specific [aspects] of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
The *Miaozong* (Exquisite Commentary) states: "Vairocana pervades all places; all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.

What is called the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither self nor other, neither cause nor fruit; it is the substance of perfect, eternal great enlightenment. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* says:
"That which is called the meaning of 'enlightenment' refers to the essence of mind being free from thought; being free from thought..."
The marks [of the Buddha] are equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere; the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body.

Because it is based upon this Dharma-body that the term "original enlightenment" (benjue) is spoken, we know that the perfectly luminous essence of the Original Buddha is the inherent nature-virtue (xingde) possessed by us ordinary beings.
Therefore, all the practices taught in the various teachings are nothing other than means for manifesting this.
Because they share the same essence of awakening, these four samādhis are collectively termed "Buddha-recollection" (buddhānusmṛti); however, their gateways of contemplative method differ.

For instance, the *ekavyūha-samādhi* involves directly contemplating the three paths to manifest the Buddha of the fundamental nature; the *vaipulya-samādhi* combines the recitation of dhāraṇīs; the *saddharma-puṇḍarīka-samādhi* combines the recitation of the sutra with contemplation;

and the *avalokiteśvara-samādhi* combines counting the breath with the mindfulness of the awakened mind (*bodhyaṅga*) throughout the three natures. These samādhis are practiced by traversing various phenomena.
Although they differ, these various forms of mindfulness of the Buddha are identical in that they all serve to reveal the essence of Great Enlightenment.

While all such practices of mindfulness of the Buddha generally reveal the essence of all Buddhas, this specific contemplative gate and the Pratyutpanna Samādhi rely upon the objective environment and the personal embodiment of the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī;
by employing subtle and wondrous contemplation, they focus specifically on Amitābha to reveal the true essence of the Buddha. Although they rely upon that external realm, it must...

Know that the environment and its inhabitants dwell together within the single mind; the nature of the mind is all-pervasive, such that there is no phenomenon it does not create and no phenomenon it does not possess.
If even a single hair’s breadth of a phenomenon were to arise from outside the mind, it could not be called the Mahayana contemplation.
The four lands are: first, the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages; second, the Land of Traceless Skillful Means; third, the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction;

and fourth, the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. Regarding the first, the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages, it is further divided into two categories; the first is called the Impure Land of Common Abode.
That is to say, among those who dwell therein, such as those in the Sahā world, there are both ordinary beings and sages; this is called "co-residence.

As for the "Pure Land of Co-residence," although its karmic fruition is exceptionally superior—such as in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—it is nonetheless a place where ordinary beings and sages co-reside. Why is this?
Because those born in that land are not necessarily all individuals who have attained the Way; it also includes those of the Two Vehicles who possess the two remaining types of skillful means.

The land where Bodhisattvas dwell is called the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya*) because they cultivate the path of expedients to sever the delusions of the four abodes; it is called "having a remainder" because ignorance has not yet been exhausted.
Third, the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas who are solely of the Dharma-body.
Fourth, the Land of Constant Quiescence and Light is the dwelling place of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. [The *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* was originally for the sake of Wei...]

Ti-xi (Dīrghanakha) detested dwelling in the defiled realm and sought to dwell in the pure realm; thus, he spoke of wondrous contemplation. This is because the three contemplations can destroy the three delusions.

It is not that they induce only rebirth in the Pure Land of the Shared Realm (*sābhāsagatika-sahā-loka*); rather, according to the depth or shallowness of the delusions severed, one naturally induces rebirth in the three [other] lands, such as the Land of Residual Existence (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
It is like needing medicine to restore the body: having obtained a formula for immortality, one compiles and synthesizes it.
Wearing this not only brings peace to the body but can also make the bones light.

For those who practice the "Mind-Only Pure Land" (Vijñaptimātra), a single thought-moment is as if there were one lamp in the East and another lamp in the West of Amitābha’s Pure Land; it is because of this that...
Because light pervades everywhere, the one is all and all is one. Outside of mind there is no land; outside of land there is no mind.
This is the realm of phenomena, the Pure Land of Mind-Only. Because it is neither destroyed nor confused, this lamp and that lamp do not interfere with one another.
Mind is simply mind; Buddha is simply Buddha; the Pure Land is simply the Pure Land. It is precisely this.
Sentient beings of this land who mindfully recollect the Buddha of that land and seek rebirth therein—this is the "principle within the phenomenon" (li-zhi) regarding the Western Pure Land.

Although one distinguishes between principle and phenomenon, they are in reality not two separate paths. If one is restricted to the Western Land alone without realizing it is Mind-Only, then one attains the phenomenon but loses the principle.
Nevertheless, even if one has not yet attained accord with principle, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, one still attains rebirth there, even while remaining [in this world].
Even those of the lower grade do not undergo retrogression; yet, if one restricts oneself to the mind alone and does not seek the Western Land, one loses both the phenomenal and the noumenal.
Because one does not seek rebirth, one fails to attain it—this is the loss regarding the phenomenon (*dharma*).

Because one does not know that there are no phenomena outside the mind, one dogmatically clings to the square inch of the heart as being the "mind," thereby obscuring the principle of the perfect interfusion of mind and dharmas—this is the loss regarding the noumenon (*tattva*).
Substituting Principle for Phenomena:

The Sixth Patriarch said, "If people in the East commit offenses and create karma while seeking rebirth in the West, and if people in the West likewise commit offenses and create karma, where would they seek rebirth? Furthermore, Master Zhigong said, "The wise person..."
To know that the mind is the Buddha is the teaching for the wise; for the foolish, there is the aspiration to go to the Western Land.

What both masters have said uses principle to subsume phenomena, serving as medicine according to the ailment. If one generates understanding merely by following the words, then grasping at the medicine becomes the disease itself.

If one speaks directly from the standpoint of principle, not a single dharma can be apprehended; what pure land could there be to be born in? Not only is there no pure land, but [the self... is likewise non-existent.
The mind, too, cannot be apprehended, and this non-apprehension itself cannot be apprehended.
If this is so, then what is called "the Western Land within one's own mind" and the claim that "the mind itself is Buddha" would both become mere excrescences.

From the *Introduction to the Compendium of the Essential Teachings on the Samantabhadra-buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, citing the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*: "There are three powers for rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha.
The first is the power of the originally existing Buddha-nature; this refers to the Tathāgatagarbha within the mind of afflictions."

Second is the power of the compassionate light that gathers and protects; this refers to Amitābha’s immeasurable radiance, which gathers in and never abandons those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Third is the power of the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha; this refers to the fact that by recollecting and mindfully contemplating the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and the future.
These three powers are like three strands of rope joined together to form a single great cord, capable of pulling heavy loads.
Furthermore, objects are like water, fire, or a mirror. If one holds a mirror toward the sun and uses moxa to catch it, one can obtain fire;

if one holds it toward the moon and uses a pearl to catch it, one can obtain water. Now, using the mirror’s inherent nature of possessing both water and fire as a metaphor, it represents the power of the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by sentient beings.
The necessity of relying on the light of the sun or moon to illuminate it is a metaphor for Amitābha.
The power of being gathered by the light of compassion; the analogy that a pearl and mugwort can summon water and fire represents the power of faith and mindfulness of the Buddha.
These three factors of the Buddha are indispensable; only when these three things harmonize will water and fire arise.
When these three powers assist one another, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land.
When the water is clear, the moon appears.
The layman Yang Wuyi said: "The Great Vow Sage comes from the Pure Land, yet in coming there is truly no coming;

the ordinary person of deep resolve goes to the Pure Land, yet in going there is truly no going. He does not come here, and this one does not go there; yet the ordinary person [perceives it otherwise]."
Why is it that in this holy assembly we encounter one another and attain communion? The radiance of Amitābha is like the pure, full moon, universally illuminating the ten directions.
When water is clear and still, the moon manifests its entire form; yet the moon does not suddenly come there to take up the water.
When water is turbid and moving, the moon has no fixed reflection; yet the moon does not suddenly depart from the water to abandon it.
Master Tianyi Huai asked his students, "If one says that one discards the defiled to take up the pure, this belongs to deluded thought;
yet if one says there is no Pure Land, this contradicts the Buddha’s words. How should those who cultivate the Pure Land practice? The assembly was silent. He then answered for them himself:
"When born, one is certainly born; when departing, one truly does not go. He further said: "It is like a wild goose flying over the Long [River]."
The empty reflection sinks into the cold water, where the wild geese have ceased leaving tracks; the water has no intention to retain the shadow.

Expansive and narrow are both at ease, for the ten directions of the Dharma-realm do not depart from a single mote of dust; thus, a single mote of dust, though infinitesimal, is equal in measure to the Buddha’s Dharma-realm.
Though lands are vast, they do not depart from a single speck of dust; though the distance to the ten directions extends for a hundred thousand leagues, it does not exceed the space of a square inch.

There is no interval between past and present, because the three periods of time do not depart from a single thought-moment; thus, the three periods are all ungraspable, as the fundamental nature of worldly phenomena is in constant flux.
Because it is eternally abiding, the Sūtra says: "Contemplating that which is remote as if it were this very day;
in a mere moment, one passes before all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions with a single mind, undisturbed."

Zhenxie said: "The Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation is a direct path for cultivation that connects with those of the highest faculties, while also drawing in those of middling and inferior capacities.
Therefore, the teaching of 'single-mindedness without distraction' encompasses two meanings: single-mindedness in principle (*li*) and single-mindedness in phenomena (*shi*).
As for single-mindedness in phenomena, everyone is capable of practicing it; it requires only a single moment of mindfulness, like a dragon regaining the water."
The tiger relying on the mountain refers to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "If one recollects the Buddha and thinks of the Buddha, whether in the present or the future, one will certainly see the Buddha;
without relying on expedient means, one will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind. As for single-mindedness through principle, this is also not some other method;

it simply takes the four characters "A-mi-t'o-fo" as the *huatou* (critical phrase), and throughout the two-and-six hours of the day—from the moment of the ten recitations at dawn—directly applies it.

Awakening [to this] is not through the thought of having a mind, nor through the thought of having no mind, nor through the thought of both having and not having a mind, nor through the thought of neither having nor not having a mind.
With the severance of the limits of past and future, when not a single thought arises, one transcends all stages and suddenly leaps to the Buddha-ground.
Is this not the vision of the Buddha in the Pure Land being simpler than in the Chan school? One can truly know that...
Whether in the teachings or in Chan, the Buddhas and patriarchs all cultivated pure karma and shared the same single vow;
once one enters this gate, one can enter all infinite Dharma gates.
In daily life, one should maintain focused mindfulness.

Ciyun said: Whenever one engages in worldly affairs, if the inner mind does not forget the Buddha and recollects the Pure Land—just as when a person’s mind is preoccupied with a pressing matter, and though they pass through various activities such as speaking, coming and going, sitting, and lying down, it does not hinder their secret recollection of that prior concern—likewise, the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha should be maintained in this way; or, should it be lost...

One should repeatedly bring the mind back through mindfulness until it becomes habitual over time, so that one spontaneously and constantly remains mindful. Furthermore, if even a slight unwholesome thought arises in the mind, one should immediately recollect the Buddha;

by the power of the Buddha, those unwholesome thoughts will naturally subside. If one sees others suffering, with a mind of mindfulness toward the Buddha, one should feel compassion for them and vow that they may be freed from suffering.
As the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* states: "If one wishes to engage in unwholesome dharmas..."
All unfulfilled roots of goodness will be swiftly accomplished; through such continuous mindfulness of the Buddha and binding the mind thereto, one can accomplish all causes and merits of purity.
Longshu said: Whenever one hears an evil sound, one should recite the name of Amitābha Buddha to dispel and ward it off.
One should vow that all people shall not engage in evil deeds. Whenever one sees a virtuous act, one should then recite...
Through Amitābha Buddha’s vow of assistance, may all people perform virtuous deeds;
when there is no other business, silently recite the name of Amitābha Buddha constantly before one's eyes so that it is never forgotten from moment to moment.
Those who can do this will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
The *Sleeping-Time Contemplation and Great Collection of Sūtras Liturgy for Repentance* states: "Those who practice the Pure Land, when entering contemplation or during sleep,
should first stand up, join their palms, and with single-minded devotion face west and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times, [invoking] Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
When the assembly of the pure ocean had finished, they immediately made this vow: "We disciples are currently ordinary beings whose karmic offenses are deep and heavy;

we transmigrate through the six realms and cannot escape. Now, having encountered a virtuous friend and heard the name and title of Amitābha’s merits, we single-mindedly recite it, vowing to be born in the Pure Land.
We pray that the Buddha will take pity on us, extend his hand, and guide us across. We disciples do not know [the way]..."
The World-Honored One Amitābha’s physical marks, radiance, vows, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, manifestations of their forms,
and the adornments of their lands— having spoken these words, if one enters contemplation with single-minded right mindfulness,
or during sleep, or at the very moment of making the vow, one will see various auspicious signs; whether seen within contemplation or within dreams, this is so.
Lately, the Dharma has manifested great efficacy, which I cannot describe in detail; practice it with diligence, and you will surely find that faith is not in vain.

For those who follow the Perfect and Sudden teaching and deny cause and effect, whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, they must all abide by the holy teachings so as to fully accord with the Buddha’s mind. If one practices *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha’s name)...

If giving rise to thoughts and stirring the mind constitutes deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), then even ceasing the mind and remaining without thought likewise becomes deluded conceptualization.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly dwell in profound seclusion, it would still be a mere shadow of the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).
If those who recite the Buddha's name suffer from the affliction of attachment to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), then those who cling to emptiness suffer an even greater affliction. Forever...
Jiashan said: "To recklessly dismiss emptiness and cast aside cause and effect is to wander aimlessly and invite calamity. To abandon the manifest and cling to emptiness is likewise a sickness;

it is like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into a fire. If seeking a Buddha elsewhere outside is considered a failure to reach the truth, then clinging internally to one's own mind is an even greater failure.
Changsha said: "The student of the Way does not recognize the Real, precisely because they follow..."
Come to know that the fundamental ignorance of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas is what ignorant people call the "original person.
If seeking a Pure Land elsewhere is considered a biased view, then those who cling to the present moment as the Pure Land commit an even greater error.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that those who fall into the way of demons all point to the present as the Buddha-land, claiming there is no separate Pure Abode.
The one with the golden-colored mark speaks favorably of the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue, claiming they are all pure lands; he asserts that the male and female organs are themselves bodhi.
Both disciple and master fall into royal peril, falling into the Avīci Hell through delusion and ignorance.

If one claims that the cultivation and realization of existence is a provisional teaching, yet clings to the non-existence of cultivation and realization, one falls into the ranks of external paths; the calamity of this is even greater.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Such a person initially does not realize they are possessed by a demon; they claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

They believe that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment. In their hearts, they hold even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt, let alone those of lower status such as *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
They do not pay homage to stupas and temples, and they destroy scriptures and images, claiming they are merely made of gold, copper, clay, or wood."
To fail to show reverence for one's own physical body—which is truly eternal—and instead to venerate earthen and wooden images is indeed a profound perversion.

Those who hold such deep faith will follow this practice by destroying their own bodies, burying them in the ground; these deluded beings shall enter the Avīci Hell. How could one not believe the Buddha’s earnest and repeated exhortations?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the path of Māra will gradually arise to corrupt and disrupt the Buddha-dharma.
Just as fire seeks dryness and water seeks moisture, so shall malevolent spirits distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

If, throughout one's life, one maintains a pure mind, possesses firm and sincere faith, and with utmost sincerity performs prostrations, recitations, repentance, and makes vows—I know that whether in body or mind, such a person [shall be protected]."

One who shares affinity with Amitābha will be joined with him; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Just as when the wind blows and the trees lean toward the west, when they fall, they must surely topple toward the west.
Master Shou’s *Treatise on Non-Self* (this was not originally composed for the sake of the Pure Land, yet those who practice for the Pure Land must know it).

Question: Not only do those who practice virtue as non-Buddhists fail to attain liberation, but even among those who rely on the internal teaching (Buddhism), there are some who do not attain the Way.

Why is this? Answer: It is because they all maintain the notion of a self (*ātman*) that they are unable to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Whenever they act, they always think, "I am the one who acts.
They become attached to whatever they encounter, clinging to cause and effect. If one realizes the principle of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), one attains the realization of the One.
When the mind does not stir amidst the dust of afflictions, it is liberated in that very place.
Question: At the moment of actual practice, how is it that one realizes the absence of self? Answer: At the time of action, things arise from conditions;
because there is activity, yet no sovereign controller, the sounds that emerge are like wind-chimes, turning and moving according to circumstances.
It is like a wooden man who acts solely according to the power of karma, with no self-nature to be found.

The aggregation and dispersal of the four elements, their arising and ceasing in accordance with conditions, and even the taking of bodies within the six realms of existence are likewise thus; in reality, there is no person who can come or go.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Just as a mechanical wooden man can produce various sounds, yet it has neither self nor non-self."
The nature of my karma is also like this. A treatise states: "By reason of causes and conditions one is born in heaven; by reason of causes and conditions one falls into hell.
If it were said that the "self" is not dependent on causes and conditions, then why would one who commits evil not be born in heaven but instead fall into hell?
Would I ever desire to suffer in that hell? Since I have committed evil yet do not experience pleasure, we know for certain that [it is the result of] good [karma].

The retribution for evil feelings arises solely from causes and conditions; it is not "I. Yet, amidst this absence of self and absence of agency, sentient beings falsely identify with a self and its actions, arrogantly asserting themselves as masters.
They do not realize that these are the workings of consciousness; there is absolutely no creator.
All non-Buddhists claim that because they grasp at action, there must be a divine self (*puruṣa*). If there were no divine self, who would be the agent of these actions? This is what wisdom knows.
The refutation states: Since the mind is of the nature of cognition and perception, it can itself cause the body to act without depending on a self (ātman).

It is like the nature of fire, which can burn objects without requiring a person. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Regarding the substantially existent self-body that you maintain, is it possessed of thought or devoid of thought?
If it possesses thought, it must be impermanent, because it does not possess thought at all times."
Because it is devoid of thought like space, the self cannot perform actions nor receive their results; therefore, the reasoning for the existence of such a grasped self is in both cases untenable.

From this, one should know that there is certainly no real self, but only the various consciousnesses which, from beginningless time, have arisen in succession as cause and effect—preceding moments perishing and succeeding moments arising.
Through the habitual perfuming of delusion, they manifest as if possessing the characteristics of a self, and the foolish falsely cling to them therein.

That which is both "mine" and "not-self" is precisely the nature of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). This nature is the essence (*tattva*), and essence carries the meaning of the fundamental substance.
Since every dharma is produced from a multitude of conditions, it truly lacks an intrinsic essence. Because there is no essence, it is empty.
Therefore, sentient beings cling to this emptiness of nature as being substantially real; internally, they are bound by the notion of "mine," and externally, they are fettered by sensory objects.
The scope of what is practiced does not transcend the mind and its objects; even when the fruit is attained, it does not depart from its cause.

Although the stages of ascent and descent differ, one remains constantly bound to the various realms of existence, fluctuating between high and low. Throughout the cycle of birth and death, all manner of afflictions arise, and "I" am their root.
Question: Since all phenomena lack intrinsic substance and are originally empty by nature, how can there be the establishment of various phenomena?
Answer: It is precisely because they are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature that they arise from conditions. If they possessed an intrinsic substance, they would not depend on conditions to arise;

since they do not arise independently of conditions, the myriad phenomena possess a determinate nature. If one were to establish fixed characteristics, it would result in the fault of eternalism. Thus it is well said: [the text continues with a verse].
Evil cannot be altered, yet cause and effect thus become disordered: one who commits evil should be born in heaven, while one who performs good should sink into the abyss.
Because there is no cause, performing good should yield no merit, and committing evil should entail no guilt;
because there is no fruit, all phenomena (dharmas) lack substance and fixed nature, appearing only through conditions. Since they arise from conditions, all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature.

Because emptiness is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it establishes the various phenomena that arise through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that Bodhisattvas establish all Buddha-activities within the absence of self-nature.
Therefore, existence is established by means of emptiness; "existence" and "non-existence" are merely conventional names.
From existence, one discerns emptiness, for emptiness has no independent essence of its own.
Question: How is it that the manifestation of all phenomena is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)? Answer: Because arising itself is non-arising, they are without intrinsic nature.
If one says there is arising, does it arise from itself, from another, from both, or without a cause?
If one says it arises from itself—for example, as with one's own body—if it were not produced by parents, how could it have arisen? Therefore, it is said: "This very body..."

The physical body inherited from one’s parents arises through the convergence of internal and external causes and conditions: past karma serves as the internal cause, while reliance upon the parents’ bodies serves as the external condition.
Thus, it does not arise from itself, nor is it said to be produced by another; for if there were no prior karma as its own internal cause, it would never take on a womb.
It exists solely through the power of one’s own karma, just as external factors such as earth and water cannot produce [a sprout] if they lack [the seed].
If seeds were determined not to arise, or if they arose through co-production, how could there be the function of an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) established by means of causes and conditions?
Since conditions arise from causes and lack the capacity for external assistance, and since causes and conditions are each individually incapable of union, how could there be such a thing?

It is like a single grain of sand having no oil; even if many are gathered together, there is still no oil. It is like a single blind man who cannot see; even if a multitude of blind men are assembled, how could they see? If [it were so], it would be the same.
That which arises without a cause is like the son of a barren woman or a whisk made of tortoise hair; if even that which has a cause does not exist, how could that which lacks a cause exist?
Furthermore, since one posits "no-cause" based on "having-a-cause," and since "having-a-cause" is non-existent, "no-cause" is also extinguished.
Once one realizes that both the positions of self and other are without arising, all four positions are refuted. Since neither self nor other exists, who is there to perform the conjunction?

Because there is no cause, there are four propositions; that which is naturally quiescent is known as the arising of non-arising, wherein illusory appearances are vividly manifest, while the true nature of the non-arising of arising is profoundly still.
Thus, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "The meaning of that which is produced by causes and conditions is the cessation of meaning, not the cessation of birth;
the meaning of all births and cessations is the arising of meaning, not its cessation."
Question: Since all dharmas are without intrinsic nature and without arising, why do sentient beings cling to objective conditions and thereby receive real retribution?
Answer: It is precisely because they do not understand the absence of intrinsic nature and are deluded into regarding things as truly existent that they receive real retribution.
If one realizes that their nature is empty, then craving and attachment will not arise; since one does not indulge in such attachment, one acts spontaneously and dwells nowhere.
Because its cause ultimately does not receive a fruit, the Sūtra says, "When the mind arises, all phenomena arise," and it also says, "All things are created solely by the mind.
If the mind does not arise, external objects are eternally void; realizing that the nature of objects is empty, the mind becomes naturally quiescent.

Once the deluded mind is stilled, how could illusory appearances arise? When both mind and objects are merged in obscurity, one spontaneously accords with the Way. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The eyes, ears..."

The faculties of nose, tongue, body, mind, and the mental consciousness—all are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature; it is only through the discriminating activity of the deluded mind that they are perceived as existing. It is further said:
"All phenomena in the world take the mind as their master; according to how one interprets them, one grasps at various marks, which are inverted and do not accord with reality."
Question: Since one has already received actual retribution, why do you say that all things are empty? Answer:

It is clearly stated that sentient beings delusively perceive their own nature as real, yet its nature is eternally empty. Although they undergo suffering and pleasure, and feelings of aversion and attachment arise, both person and phenomena are empty;
there is nothing to be attained. This is like seeing good or evil in a dream, where joy and sorrow fill the heart; yet upon waking, everything is suddenly gone.
When the perception of objects arises, it is not existent; within the dream, it is not non-existent. Since one has practiced the causes of perversion, there is no lack of the fruit of delusion.

Question: As for the forgetting of the mind and the illusory objects, were they originally non-existent, or do they become non-existent from this day forward? Answer: Mind and objects are fundamentally non-existent.
Question: Since sentient beings have fundamentally never existed, why do they not attain liberation? Answer: Since there is fundamentally no bondage, how can one speak of "liberation"?
It is simply because they fail to realize that which is fundamentally non-existent and falsely give rise to the notion of present existence.

Due to the power of habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time, they remain unaware and unknowing, revolving according to karma; yet, though constrained by karma, their nature remains eternally pure.

Question: How does one attain ultimate purity? Answer: There are two aspects to this. First, by realizing that [the mind] was originally non-existent, one attains self-nature purity (*svabhāva-viśuddhi*).
Second, by purifying delusional defilements, one attains stainless purity (*vimala-viśuddhi*). Once the fundamental nature is pure, delusive thoughts do not arise;

the two obstacles are simultaneously extinguished, and the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are thoroughly clarified. Thus, one accords with the source of original luminosity, where both seeds and manifestations are stilled.
The Western Direct Pointing, Volume Upper;
The Western Direct Pointing, Volume Middle.
Compiled by the Layman Yinnan.
The scriptures and treatises point toward the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
where the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra exhorts the youth Sudhana and the great assembly of the ocean-like gathering to make the ten great vows.
When the time of death arrives and all the sense faculties are completely dispersed and destroyed, and all majestic powers are entirely...
Even if they should fall away from their practice, as long as they do not abandon this King of Vows, he will lead them at all times;

in a single kṣaṇa, they shall attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss. They will see for themselves that they have been born within a lotus flower and received a prophecy of enlightenment from the Buddha.
After the passing of countless kalpas, throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds in the ten directions, they will...
Through the power of wisdom, they act for the benefit of sentient beings in accordance with their minds;

even within the great ocean of suffering of the afflictions, they are able to rescue and deliver sentient beings, enabling them to transcend [suffering] and all attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "One who hears this sutra and practices according to its teachings will, at the end of life here, be reborn in the world of peace and bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), the abode of Amitābha Buddha and the great bodhisattvas.
One shall be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne, attaining the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, the faculty of the eye becomes pure; by means of this purity..."
With the faculty of the eye, one beholds seven million two thousand *koṭis* of *nayutas* of *Ganges-sand*-like Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
As the verse says:
"If a person, with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and once utters 'Namo Buddhāya'..."
"All have already attained the Buddha-way.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Mahāsthāmaprāpta said to the Buddha: "I recall that in the past, as many kalpas ago as there are sands in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitābha.
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of a single kalpa; the last of these Buddhas was named Transcending the Sun and Moon."

“Kāśyapa, my teaching of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) is like this: suppose there are two people, one who is single-mindedly mindful and one who is single-mindedly forgetful.
Even if these two meet, they do not truly meet; even if they see each other, it is as if they do not see.

If these two remember each other and their mutual remembrance is deep, then from birth to birth they will be like a form and its shadow, never separated from one another throughout the ten directions.”
He comes to pity and cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. Even if the child flees and wanders away, what does the mother’s remembrance achieve?

But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers him, then throughout successive lives, mother and child will not be separated by great distance. If sentient beings with their own minds remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present or in the future;
they will not be far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, they will spontaneously attain the mind [of enlightenment].
It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense; their body possesses a fragrant scent. This is what is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.

Originally, when I was on the ground of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha. Now, within this realm, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "If there are good men or good women who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and hold it in mind—
whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days—
with single-mindedness and without distraction, then at the time of their death, Amitābha Buddha, together with [his assembly...]"

When such a person stands before the assembly of noble ones at the time of death, their mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Śāriputra, because I see this benefit, I speak these words:
if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should resolve to be born in that land.
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* states: The Buddha told Maitreya, "In this world, there are seventy-two billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
the number of bodhisattvas of minor practice is beyond reckoning. It is not only in my land that this is so;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable multitudes of great bodhisattvas all keep Amitābha in mind."
One should aspire to go to the land of Amitābha Buddha.

The *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations* states: "If a good man or a good woman merely hears the name of the Buddha and the names of these two Bodhisattvas, they will eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas; how much more so if they practice mindfulness and recite 'Namo Amitābha Buddha'?"
Upon hearing this single sound, one should know that this person is a *puṇḍarīka* lotus among men, with Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva as their supreme friends.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If a person recollects the Buddha even with a distracted mind, they shall be freed from suffering and their merit shall never be exhausted; how much more so if they do so with a concentrated mind?"
He thought to himself, "Is this the Buddha?
According to the *Hukong jing* (Sūtra on Protecting the Mouth), there was an evil ghost whose form was hideous and foul; its body emitted fierce flames while its mouth disgorged maggots.
Wailing aloud, it ran hither and thither. At that time, the Arhat Pūrṇa asked it, "What sins did you commit in your past lives?"
"Now experiencing this suffering," the hungry ghost replied, "in a former life I was once a śramaṇa who uttered an evil word to obstruct another's cultivation of goodness;
thus I have now encountered this suffering. Venerable sir, when you return to Jambudvīpa, please admonish the bhikṣus:
whenever you see others performing even a hair’s breadth of wholesome deeds, you should only rejoice and assist them, never causing them to be thwarted or fail, lest you fall into my state."
These evil beings have undergone suffering for many tens of millions of kalpas; even if they should escape their ghostly forms, they will enter hell again.
At that time, the hungry ghosts, having spoken these words, wailed and threw themselves to the ground like a great mountain collapsing.
Hearing such words, one’s heart is truly chilled with dread. If uttering a single evil word leads a ghost to endure such suffering for many kalpas, how much more so for those who obstruct others?
Bow to the Buddha and recite His name!
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states that when one recites the Buddha’s name with a loud voice, the demonic armies will retreat and scatter.

The *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that because sentient beings are dull-witted and cannot understand through visualization, one should simply ensure that the sound of the recitation continues without interruption.
One will naturally attain rebirth in the Buddha-land.

The *Ratnarāśi-śāstra* states: "One who bathes in the great ocean has already utilized the waters of the hundred rivers; likewise, one who recites the name of the Buddha will necessarily achieve samādhi.
This is just as when a clear pearl is cast into turbid water—the turbid water cannot fail to become clear—and so too when the recitation of the Buddha's name is cast [into the mind].
One with a distracted mind cannot fail to attain Buddhahood.

The *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) asks: "If the nature of names is empty and thus cannot express or explain the teachings of the dharmas, what is the difference between exclusively reciting the Buddha's name and speaking of food to satisfy hunger?
The answer is: If one says that names are useless and cannot express the dharmas...
Since the substance itself should also summon water and fire, we know that the trap and snare are not empty; thus the fish and rabbit are caught. Question:
For what reason can the power of a single recitation of the Buddha cut through all obstacles? Answer:

A single grain of sandalwood transforms a forest of *eranda* trees forty *yojana*s in extent so that it becomes entirely fragrant. It is also like a person who uses a lion’s sinew as a lute string; its sound...
When one string is struck, all the other strings are completely severed and destroyed.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is the unsurpassed Dharma King, and the great Bodhisattvas serve as his Dharma ministers;
that which is honored by these ministers is solely the Dharma King. There was once a Bodhisattva who reflected upon how he had slandered the *Prajñāpāramitā* in the past..."
If one falls into the evil realms and undergoes immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas, even if one subsequently practices other paths, one cannot escape the sea of suffering;
yet, if later one encounters a virtuous friend who teaches one to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, one will immediately have one’s karmic obstacles extinguished and be reborn in the Pure Land.
I now ought to pay homage in gratitude to Amitābha Buddha. Why is this? Because he is our parent.

Neither my kinsmen nor the heavenly kings and others can deliver me from this sea of suffering; it is only through the power of Amida Buddha’s vow to embrace me that I am able to escape this sea of suffering.
A verse says: "If a person vows to become a Buddha and mindfully recollects Amida, they shall immediately attain his manifestation.
Therefore, I take refuge in him and pay homage. Furthermore, it is said that in the world of the Buddha, there was an old man who sought [liberation].
The renunciant Śāriputra did not permit the Buddha to observe this man; however, in a past kalpa, while gathering firewood, he was pursued by a tiger and climbed a tree.
As his voice failed him, he cried out "Namo Buddha. Possessing this slight merit, he encountered the Buddha and attained deliverance, obtaining the fruit of Arhatship. Alas!
If even a single invocation of His name can lead to liberation, how much more so for one who recollects the Buddha throughout their entire life?
The *Vajracchedikā Sūtra Ritual Manual* states: "Even wild foxes listened to Baizhang’s Dharma-conch; the snail still protects the *Vajracchedikā*;
ten thousand wandering fish, hearing the Buddha’s name, were transformed into deva sons; five hundred bats, hearing the sound of the Dharma, all became sages and worthies;
the python heard the repentance ritual and was reborn in heaven; the dragon listened to the Dharma and awakened to the Way. If even such creatures as these were able to comprehend and realize it,"
How much more so should humans not turn their hearts to recite the Buddha’s name?
The "Chapter on the Difficulty of Hearing the True Dharma" states:

"The Buddha said that if people of the world hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, with a heart of compassion and joy, their will becomes pure, their hair stands on end, and tears immediately flow, they have all [practiced] for many successive lifetimes."
One who constantly practices the Buddha-way is no ordinary person. If you do not believe the Buddha’s words, do not trust the Buddha’s teachings, and do not believe in rebirth—
knowing that you have all come from the evil realms with residual karmic retribution yet to be exhausted and ignorance still unresolved—
I shall therefore preach this Great Dharma for you all, so that you may behold Amitābha Buddha and his land.
At the end of life, the retribution for good and evil is distinguished by its excellence or inferiority.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "In all the worlds, birth and death continue in succession;

birth arises from habitual tendencies, and death proceeds from the flow of transformation. At the moment of death, before the warmth has departed, the good and evil of one's entire life manifest simultaneously."
If one’s present thoughts are purely conceptual, they will immediately fly upward and be born in the heavens.

If, while flying, the mind is accompanied by both merit and wisdom, as well as pure vows, the mind will naturally open and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands, being reborn therein according to one’s wishes.

If the emotional aspect is slight and the conceptual aspect is predominant, one will rise lightly without traveling far, becoming a Flying Immortal (*fei-xian*). If the emotional and conceptual aspects are equal, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among humans.

Those with intermittent thoughts and clear intelligence are clever, while those with obscure thoughts and dull intelligence are obtuse. Those with many thoughts and few feelings flow into the realm of horizontal birth;

the heavy become the fur-bearing beasts, and the light become the winged tribes. Those with seven feelings and three thoughts sink beneath the water wheel and are born at the edge of fire, receiving their breath from fierce flames and taking bodies as hungry ghosts.
Constantly burned by fire, they can be harmed by water itself; without food or drink, they pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
In the nine kalpas of the hell where one thought of emotion remains, those who sink downward through the wheel of fire are reborn in two types of hells:
the Intermittent and the Uninterrupted. Those of pure emotion sink directly into the Avīci Hell.
