If, within their sinking minds, they have slandered the Mahāyāna, violated the Buddha’s prohibitions, spoken deceptive and false teachings, greedily misappropriated offerings of faith, unworthily accepted veneration, or committed the five heinous crimes and ten grave offenses, they shall be reborn there once more.
Regarding the Avīci Hell:

The *Sūtra on the Protector of the Realm* records the Buddha saying: "If, at the time of death, a person knows in advance that their end has arrived and maintains clear right mindfulness, they bathe, put on clean robes, and pass away with auspiciousness.
Light shall illuminate their body, and they will behold the marks and signs of the Buddhas."
If one possesses both goodness and meditative concentration, it is certain that this person will be reborn in the Pure Land.
If a person recites the Buddha’s name and maintains the precepts but lacks a mind of diligent effort, then at the end of life they will have neither auspicious signs nor inauspicious signs;

such a person is not received by the Underworld nor taken up by the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, departing as if falling asleep. Because this person has not severed their doubts, they will be born in the City of Doubt and enjoy happiness there for five hundred years.

If one cultivates faith and aspiration once more, one shall surely return to the Pure Land. If a person gives rise to a heart of compassion and maintains right mindfulness, having no attachment to wealth, treasures, wife, or children;
if their vision is pure and they look upward with a smile, contemplating the celestial palaces where the deities will come to welcome them;
if they hear celestial music with their ears and see celestial youths with their eyes—upon casting off this retribution body, they will certainly be reborn in the heavenly realms. If...
If one gives rise to a supple mind and a mind of merit, remains free from physical illness, recollects one’s parents and spouse,
is not confused regarding good and evil, maintains a straightforward mind, and departs after entrusting one’s household wealth and bidding farewell, one will certainly be reborn in the human realm.
If a person looks upon their own kinsmen with an evil eye, raises their hand to stroke empty space, or urinates or defecates [inappropriately], [they shall suffer].

He becomes aware that his body and breath are foul and filthy, and his two eyes are red and inflamed; he lies prostrate with his face down, curled up on his left side, with pain in all his hundred joints.
Or he may see ominous signs, unable to speak, groaning and crying out as his karmic debts and grievances manifest before him.

His consciousness becomes scattered, deluded, and inverted; his entire body feels like ice, his hands clench into death-grips, and his body becomes as hard as stone—this person’s life [is at its end].

One who will certainly enter hell is a person who likes to lick their lips, whose body burns like fire, who constantly suffers from hunger and thirst, who speaks of food and drink, who keeps their mouth open without closing it, and who is greedily attached to wealth and treasures;
when their life ends, they find it difficult to pass away and depart with eyes wide open—such a person will certainly enter the realm of hungry ghosts.
If a person is afflicted by a grave illness, as if shrouded in clouds and mist, their mind and spirit become confused and scattered, and they are filled with fear.
If one hears the names of the Buddhas yet still craves the taste of flesh and blood, refuses to accept exhortations to virtue, remains attached to wife and children,
curls their fingers and toes, perspires all over the body, utters coarse and raspy sounds, and froths at the mouth— when these signs manifest before them,
they will certainly enter the realm of animals.

Regarding the ten kinds of obstacles and difficulties, the *Qun yilun* (Treatise on the Multitude of Doubts) states that there are ten types of people in the world who are unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha at the time of death:

first, because they may not necessarily encounter virtuous friends, there is no principle for them to receive exhortation to mindfulness; second, because the suffering of karma entangles their bodies, they have no leisure to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Third, those who suffer from a stroke and lose the power of speech, unable to invoke the Buddha’s name; fourth, those who are deranged and lose their minds, making it difficult for them to focus their thoughts;

fifth, those who encounter water or fire and have no leisure to practice with sincerity; sixth, those who encounter wild beasts such as jackals and wolves and no longer have virtuous friends to guide them;
seventh, those whose faith is destroyed by evil associates at the moment of death; and eighth, those who overeat until they fall into a stupor and die.
Ninth, those who perish suddenly in the midst of military arrays and battle; tenth, those whose lives are destroyed by suddenly falling from high cliffs.

These ten kinds of people will, at the moment of death, certainly be unable to practice the Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*); they must therefore cultivate their practice in advance so that their pure karma (*śukla-karman*) is perfected.
Even if they encounter such difficult circumstances, they will surely receive the Buddha’s protection and deliverance.
The Patriarch’s Pointing to the Goal:
Chan Master Shou’s Four Kinds of Selections To have Chan but no Pure Land—nine out of ten go astray.

If the realm of the dead manifests before them, they are instantly carried away by it. To have no Chan but the Pure Land—of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go there. Provided one simply attains vision [of Amitābha].
Amituo, why worry about not attaining enlightenment? With both Chan and Pure Land, one is like a tiger with horns;
in this life one becomes a teacher of men, and in the next life one becomes a Buddha or Patriarch. Without both Chan and Pure Land, there are only iron beds and copper pillars;
through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there will be no one to rely upon.
Chan Master Shou’s Exhortation to Practice the Pure Land Path: Question: Regarding the merit of walking while reciting the Buddha’s name versus sitting while reciting it, how do they compare?
Answer: It is like sailing against the current; even with the sails full, one can still advance, yet if one sails with the current, the speed is easily understood.
If a single mouthful of recitation while sitting can eliminate the sins of eighty billion kalpas, how much more so the merit of reciting while walking? How could that possibly be known?

Regarding the measure [of practice], a verse says: "Walk the path five hundred times and recite the Buddha’s name one thousand times; let your activities always be thus, and the Buddha of the Western Land will naturally manifest.

(Walking the path and reciting the Buddha’s name refers to bowing to and circumambulating the Buddha while reciting; because such recitation reaches the full potential of body, speech, and mind, its merit is uniquely supreme. Master Lingzhi said:

"Ordinary worldlings of the broad earth are bound by karma and delusions, transmigrating through the five realms for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, undergoing all manner of sufferings..."
Those suffering in affliction who suddenly hear of the Pure Land and vow to seek rebirth there can transcend to that realm by reciting the Buddha’s name for even a single day;

this may be called an encounter once in a thousand lifetimes or a chance difficult to meet in ten thousand kalpas. If a person is willing to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, they will surpass all other roots of goodness;
even if one is able to practice giving, morality, meditation, and recitation, these do not equal the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name.
Prosecutor Yang said: "The Buddha Śākyamuni is the Great Teacher who points toward the Pure Land as the Land of Peace and Bliss;
Amitābha Buddha is the Teacher of that Pure Land. If you sentient beings are born in that land, there will be no sufferings whatsoever.
If you do not hear of or know this, you are truly to be pitied. Furthermore, there are virtuous persons who give rise to the three kinds of mind yet do not seek rebirth there."
What is most lamentable is threefold: first, that my Way transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs, and thus the Pure Land is not a place where one should be born;
second, that every place is a pure land, and thus the Western Paradise need not be the destination for rebirth; third, that the Holy Realm of Ultimate Bliss cannot be reached by ordinary beings.
Now, the ocean of practice is immeasurable, and the vows of Samantabhadra are vast; though the Land of Amitābha Buddha may be empty, it remains the goal of aspiration.

Māhāyāna constantly cultivates the Pure Land. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have praised it with their broad tongues, and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions share the resolve to go there together.
If you examine yourself, who among us can compare with these sages? To say that one is unworthy to be born there—how self-deceptive is that!
As for the patriarch Nāgārjuna, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* contains a prophetic record concerning him, and he was the master of Vasubandhu’s teaching lineage.
Furthermore, the *Wuliangshou lun* contains verses on seeking rebirth, and Ci'en’s *Tongzan* begins by extolling the ten superior knowers who analyzed the principles and resolved the ten doubts;
all of them were eminent sages who through diligent effort attained rebirth. How self-deprecating it is, then, to claim that rebirth is not necessary!
Even a burning chariot can be extinguished, and a stone boat does not sink; as for those who manifest immediate retribution, none are more extreme than Zhang Kui.

To transcend to a superior realm through ten recitations while those who enter hell do so with such speed as the youth Xiongjun—only to be revived and realize the wondrous cause—is a phenomenon that the transgressions of worldly people may not necessarily match.
To say one cannot be reborn there is to utterly abandon oneself.
The Patriarch Cizhao said: "If there is practice without aspiration, that practice will surely be solitary; if there is aspiration without practice, that aspiration will surely be empty.
Now, aspiration is joy and it is desire. To desire rebirth in the Western Pure Land and to wish to behold Amitābha Buddha, one must certainly make a vow to attain rebirth there.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One who does not make great vows is possessed by Māra."
All Buddha-works arise from great vows; because one desires to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way, it is necessary to attain the Vow-Pāramitā.
Thus, Samantabhadra possesses a vast and boundless ocean of vows, and Amitābha has the six or eight gates of vows.

Therefore, it is said that the Dharma-gates are so vast that there is nothing they do not encompass. Observing those who now take refuge with faith in the Buddha’s assembly, some may be afflicted by illness.
They may resolve their minds out of suffering, or conceive the intention to repay their parents, or to protect their homes, or observe the fasts out of fear of transgressions;

in all such cultivation of wholesome conditions, they do so solely to fulfill their own worldly vows, and it is rare for anyone to make a vow for their own birth-and-death or to practice mindfulness of the Buddha with the aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land.
Often, at incense altars and ritual sites, they merely offer prayers and dedicate the merit toward these ends.
These liturgical texts merely express offerings to the divine spirits for the purpose of eliminating calamities and prolonging life;

although they claim to accumulate merit by serving the Buddha, prostrating, and burning incense, they actually contradict the fundamental intent of the sutras and repentance rites. This is why those who recite them cannot attain rebirth in the Pure Land at the moment of death.
Out of compassion, I have exhorted others to collectively resolve to seek birth in the Pure Land with the correct aspiration, vowing together to become Buddhas.
The Patriarch Jizhao spoke in verse: "All phenomena arise from the mind; All phenomena cease within the mind. Our Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, Constantly taught this very truth.

To uphold the precepts without faith or aspiration Brings only the blessings of humans and devas; When these blessings are exhausted, one undergoes saṃsāra, Whirling through it with difficulty finding escape.
To study the scriptures without the eye of wisdom Is to fail to recognize the Buddha’s profound intent; In future lives, one may obtain intelligence..."

It is taught that for one with a distracted mind, it is difficult to attain liberation; thus, it is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha to generate the aspiration for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Śākyamuni spoke this with his own golden mouth, and Amitābha personally bestowed it upon him. All Buddhas protect and keep it in mind, and all devas guard and uphold it.
It is like a poor woman whose womb conceives a Cakravartin king; the devas constantly love and protect her, yet the poor woman herself does not know that there is a noble being within her womb.
My son, the mind of this person who now practices mindfulness of the Buddha is likewise: by recollecting the Buddha and constantly being mindful of him, they shall before long attain Buddhahood.

All Buddhas will skillfully protect and sustain such a person. Though they themselves do not know that "I shall be born in the Pure Land," they will certainly come again in a future life to be born among humans.
It is like a poor man’s house where there is a hidden treasure beneath the ground, which a treasure-guarding deity constantly protects.

Just as a poor person, though protected so that they do not lose [their treasure], remains unaware that there is a treasury within their own home, and thus spends each day seeking food and clothing through hired labor to sustain themselves;
so too is the mind of this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha.
Unaware that they possess the Tathāgatagarbha, they say of themselves, "I have no share [in it]," while instead aspiring to be born in the realms of humans or devas—just like a sick person.
Within one's own home there exists a truly wondrous medicine, yet being ignorant of its wondrous nature, one cannot cure one's own illness;
day after day, by one's bedside, one suffers immeasurable pain. It is the same for this person who recites the Buddha’s name:
being unaware that the mind of *nien-fo* can extinguish the diseases of greed and anger, it can act as a Great Physician King and serve as a Great Treasure Trove, benefiting and rescuing all beings.

If a person can act as a great Dharma King to protect and shelter all sentient beings, yet is still considered an ordinary being who cannot be born in the Pure Land, then even if they personally observe the fasts and precepts, they will pray for future lives to become a person of many [merits]. Many practitioners constantly speak in this way:
"If I cannot be born in this life, one failure is a hundred failures. I exhort you, O practitioner: believe me, the Tathāgata.
It is said that the Buddha has no words that are not true. When fire is fanned by the wind, its force cannot be extinguished;
fortunately, those who possess a mind of mindfulness toward the Buddha vow to transcend the three realms.
Chancellor Zheng Qingzhi exhorted people, saying: "Those who study Buddhism today do nothing more than [pursue] Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya to their ultimate conclusion."

For sudden and perfect enlightenment, nothing compares to Chan; yet those who do not possess sharp faculties and superior capacity, and who fail to grasp it through spiritual intuition and mental understanding, cannot avoid the error of falling into a stagnant void.

For the study of the Three Vehicles, nothing compares to the Teachings (Dharma); yet those who do not "forget the trap upon catching the fish" or "see the moon by following the pointing finger," cannot avoid the ailment of poring over worn-out paper.

For protecting the good and shielding against evil, nothing compares to the Vinaya; yet those whose body and mind are not pure, and whose outward appearance and inner reality do not correspond, [cannot avoid the failure of true discipline].
If one is to escape the suffering of self-entanglement, as for the gateways through which one enters, they are Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya;

and as for that to which one ultimately returns, they are Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom. Is there any way other than the single gateway of the Pure Land by which one may attain these Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom without relying upon Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya?
The *Lianzong baojian* records that a disciple asked Master Cizhao: "I, your disciple, am single-mindedly practicing the samādhi of Buddha-recitation;
may I also employ giving, upholding the precepts, making offerings, and performing meritorious deeds? The Master replied:

"If you can single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha, yet fail to uphold the precepts, you will incur the offense of transgression. If you do not practice giving, you will perpetuate stinginess and greed."
If one’s karma fails to make offerings to the Triple Gem, there will be the pride of self; if one’s karma fails to show respect to all, there will be the fault of disparaging others.
Therefore, violating the precepts leads directly to the hells, while stinginess and greed lead to rebirth as a hungry ghost.

Pride of self results in constant dwelling in the evil realms, and disparaging others results in poverty and low status life after life. These evil karmas act as an obscuration, preventing birth in a pure land.
"How could its substance be obtained?
Master Yongming Shou’s *Xinglu* (Record of His Own Practice) says: "Examine this body from dawn until noon, from noon until evening, from evening until night, and from night until dawn;
even down to a single moment, a single instant, a single thought, or a single movement."

How many minds, how many practices, how many virtues, and how many evils? How many minds desire to crush and subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), and how many minds desire to conquer the demonic adversaries?
How many minds contemplate the Triple Gem and the Four Noble Truths? How many minds realize suffering, emptiness, and impermanence?

How many minds contemplate repaying the compassionate kindness of one's parents? How many minds vow to undergo suffering on behalf of sentient beings? And how many minds resolve to cultivate the path and deeds of a Bodhisattva?
How many minds desire to practice giving and uphold the precepts? How many minds desire patience and diligence? How many minds desire meditative concentration and wisdom?
How many minds desire to compassionately rescue those in the five realms of existence? How many minds desire to exert themselves in performing what is difficult to perform?
How many minds desire to transcend and resolve what is difficult to resolve? How many minds desire to endure suffering to establish the Buddha-dharma? How many minds desire to become Buddhas?
Having already examined the mind for the sake of transforming and delivering all sentient beings, one next examines the mouth:
from dawn until this moment, how many phrases of profound meaning have been expounded? How many scriptures have been read? How many characters have been recited with understanding?
How many times has one praised the merits of the Buddha? And how many times has one performed dedication and made vows?
Next, examine the body as before at the designated times: how many times have you already bent the body to prostrate to the Buddha? How many times have you already bowed?

How many times have you already bent the body to prostrate to the Dharma and the Sangha? How many times have you already performed manual labor such as sweeping the stupas and smearing the ground with mud?
How many times have you already burned incense, scattered flowers, and lit lamps? How many times have you already swept away dust and grime and properly arranged the ritual offerings?

"How many times have I already offered worship with palms joined before banners suspended at the *stūpa*? How many times have I already circumambulated the Buddha in reverence a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times?
When he thus examines himself, he finds no merit in his own efforts; what leisure time, then, does he have to discuss the good and evil of others?
The Layman Wang of Longshu exhorted people, saying: "In the *Sutra of the Great Amitābha Buddha*, it is said that throughout the ten directions there are immeasurable Bodhisattvas..."
If even those Bodhisattvas are still desirous of being reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha, what person am I?
To provide some brief evidence, consider these cases: the later incarnation of Lord Qingsong was Zeng Gong; the later incarnation of Master Zhe suffered much grief and hardship;
the later incarnation of Old Man Gu was addicted to wealth and status; and the later incarnation of the Lotus Sutra Nun became a courtesan. All of these failed to believe.

In the Western regions, beings transmigrate through the cycle of rebirth and undergo suffering. Some say that while it is indeed difficult to realize one's nature through Zen meditation (*chán*), how does the practice of immortals (*xiān*) compare?

The answer is: To seek to learn the arts of the immortals without first cultivating the Pure Land is like discarding a magnificent jade gem at hand to search for a *wǔfū* (a low-grade stone resembling jade) whose acquisition is uncertain—is this not delusion?
According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are ten types of such immortals, all of whom possess lifespans of millions of years.
When their lifespans are exhausted, they enter the cycle of saṃsāra once more. Among those worldly people who study the arts of the immortals, not even one in ten thousand succeeds;
and even if they do succeed, they still cannot escape saṃsāra because they remain attached to form and spirit (rūpa and citta) and are unable to relinquish them.
Furthermore, form and spirit are merely delusive thoughts manifested within the true nature (bhūtadhātu). Thus, a poem by Hanshan says: "Even if you were to become an immortal..."
He resembles a corpse-guarding ghost; he does not possess the freedom from constraints found in the Buddhist tradition regarding life and death.

In recent years, the only ones who have attained immortality have been Zhongli and Lü Gong. Have you not heard how Lü Dongbin flew his sword to slay the Yellow Dragon, only to be subdued by that very dragon?
It was only upon meeting the Chan Master Huanglong that he realized his true nature and perfected the Way. Thus...
He spoke a verse, saying: "Having cast aside my gourd-bag and smashed my lute, I no longer refine mercury within the gold.
Since first beholding Huanglong, I have realized that all my previous efforts were misplaced.

Furthermore, have you not heard how the Dharma Master Tanluan of the Later Wei dynasty initially obtained ten scrolls of the *Cinnabar Scripture* from Tao Hongjing? Tanluan was delighted by this acquisition, believing that immortality could indeed be attained.
Later, while standing, he encountered the monk Bodhiruci, who asked him, "In the Buddha-way, is there eternal life? Can one ward off old age and become immortal?
Bodhiruci replied, "Eternal life and immortality—this is my Buddha-way.

He then gave him the *Sutra on the Sixteen Contemplations*, saying, "If you can recite this, then within the three realms there will be no further birth, and among the six paths there will be no further wandering through the cycles of fullness and emptiness."
News of calamity or fortune, success or failure, cannot reach him. As for his longevity, there are the *kalpa-stones* and the grains of the Ganges River;
while the number of these sands and stones is finite, the measure of his lifespan is infinite—this is the long life of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha).
Luán believed this deeply, whereupon he burned the scriptures of the immortals and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Though amidst the cold and heat...
Even when afflicted by illness, Shenluan remained diligent; the Wei Emperor, moved by his resolve, bestowed upon him the title "Divine Luan.
One day, he told his disciples, "The various sufferings of the hells must not be taken lightly; the pure karma of the nine grades must be cultivated without fail.
He then instructed his disciples to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha aloud. Luan faced west, closed his eyes, and struck [the ground].
When he died, both monastics and laypeople alike heard the sound of stringed and wind instruments coming from the west;

judging by this, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is the most direct path. Furthermore, those who attain the status of immortals keep their realizations secret and do not transmit them, claiming that to divulge the celestial mechanism (tianji) is a transgression.
In contrast, the Buddha’s Dharma-gate fears only that it will not be transmitted widely. Thus, [the Pure Land method] is straightforward.
To wish to deliver all sentient beings before one’s own completion is clearly a manifestation of vast compassion that cannot be compared to that of a divine immortal (*ṛṣi*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"When a person is born, two heavenly beings follow them—one named 'Born Together' (*Sahaja*) and the other named 'Same Name' (*Samānanāman*)."

The celestial beings constantly see humans, yet humans do not see the celestial beings; are these two celestial beings not perhaps the attendants of the two groups of youths, one virtuous and one evil?

If a person, in every thought, word, and movement, constantly keeps these two celestial beings in mind and remains thus free from shame, then practicing for the Pure Land in this manner, they will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest class. Someone might say: "How can there be two [attendants] for even a single person?"
"O Celestial Being, why is it that there are so many celestial beings? [The Buddha] replied: "When the moon universally appears in all waters, is it because there are necessarily many moons?
Day must have night; one must prepare for the night. Summer must have winter; one must prepare for the winter. Existence must have departure."

One must certainly prepare for departure. What is meant by "preparations for the night"? It refers to lamps, a solitary bed, and bedding. What is meant by "preparations for the cold"? It refers to quilts, furs, charcoal, and firewood.
What is meant by "preparations for departure"? It is merit, wisdom, and the Pure Land.
Having perused the entire Tripiṭaka, I find no mention of the theory of "depositing goods in the underworld. I therefore exhort the people of the world not to engage in such "deposits."
Regarding the funds expended, one should request monks to perform offerings for the Western Paradise; if one directs the mind single-mindedly toward the West, rebirth there is certain.
If, instead of performing meritorious deeds for the Pure Land, one establishes a "depository" for the underworld, then one’s intent lies with the underworld, and upon death, one will surely enter it.
It is like a person who, failing to practice the conduct of a gentleman, seeks to associate with the worthy and noble.
To entrust money to a jailer at the District Court, hoping that once one is imprisoned, that money will be used to avoid punishment—is this not utterly absurd?
In the course of human life, all manner of affairs weigh upon the heart; yet when the great limit of one's time arrives, they are all cast away.

When departing this world, even this body of mine is but a discarded thing; how much more so that which lies outside the body? Reflecting on this in stillness, it is as if one were in a dream. As the ancients said:
"Only when the impermanence of a single day arrives does one realize one is but a person in a dream.
Of all things, nothing can be taken along; only karma follows one. How can one not take the Pure Land as one's karma? There was an Elder named Mingliao who...
The assembly spoke in unison, pointing to this body and saying: "This is a dead thing; that which quivers within it is the living thing.
Do not make your livelihood upon the dead thing; you should make your livelihood upon the living thing. I deeply cherish these words.
For all those who covet various external objects to serve their bodies are merely making their livelihood upon the dead thing.
This is a matter of calculation.

When people see that good and evil deeds before them have not yet received their retribution, they consequently fail to believe in cause and effect, and by extension, fail to believe in the Pure Land.
Little do they realize that the fact that good and evil have not yet been repaid does not mean there will be no retribution; it is simply that the timing differs—whether sooner or later.

The Buddha once said to Ānanda: "There are those who perform good deeds in this life yet fall into hell upon death, and those who commit evil deeds in this life yet are born in heaven upon death. Ānanda asked for the reason, and the Buddha replied:

"Those who perform good deeds in this life yet fall into hell upon death are such that their goodness in this life has not yet ripened, while their evil from a previous life has already ripened. Those who commit evil deeds in this life... [and so forth].

Those born into heaven are such that the evils of their present life have not yet ripened, while the goodness of their previous lives has already matured; they receive retribution first for that which has matured.
It is like a debt: one must repay what is most urgent first. The *Zuozhuan* states that Luan Wuzi possessed such virtue that it could protect his son Yan;
although Yan committed evil, he was able to escape calamity because of it. Yan’s son Ying, however, performed good deeds, yet [the merit of the father] did not [extend to him].

The evil of this lies in its accumulation; thus, even though one may be virtuous, if it leads to calamity, such retribution for good and evil as can be seen before our eyes in the mundane world is already like this—how much more so when separated by lifetimes?
Furthermore, it is said that what the Confucian school calls "bestowing and recompense" and what the Buddhist school calls "giving and the fruit of retribution" are in fact one and the same.
The Buddha said that if one wishes to obtain grain and food, one must...
If you wish to obtain wisdom, you must diligently cultivate the fields of learning; if you wish to obtain long life, you must diligently practice the precept against killing;
if you wish to obtain wealth and honor, you must diligently practice giving. An ancient proverb says: "Everyone knows there is a coming year, so every household plants grain for the next year;
everyone knows there is a future life, so why not cultivate the merit of that future life? This is the present moment.
The blessings one receives in this life are those cultivated in a previous existence, just as the grain one consumes this year is that sown in the previous year.
Just as one cannot plant grain in the morning and eat it in the evening, so too one cannot cultivate blessings and receive their fruit immediately;
therefore, grain requires half a year to ripen, and blessings require the interval of an entire lifetime.
A person has never truly died, yet the name "death" is derived from their physical body. Why is this?
It is because when the spirit arrives and lodges within this form, the body grows through it; therefore, it is called "life.
When the spirit departs and leaves this place, the form consequently perishes; therefore, it is called "death. Thus, the spirit is the self, while the form is merely its vessel.
That which is called my "dwelling" is the body; because I have coming and going, the dwelling undergoes formation and decay.
Thus, birth is not truly birth—it is merely the form taking shape through the arrival of the spirit. Death is not truly death—it is merely the form decaying through the departure of the spirit.
The people of the world do not recognize this spirit; they see only the form, and thus they delight in life and loathe death. Is this not so?
Is it not tragic? Furthermore, when the spirit arrives, from where does it come? It comes following the conditions of one's karma (*karmapratyaya*).
When the spirit departs, to where does it go? It goes following the conditions of one's karma. What are these conditions of karma? They are the human deeds performed;
the spirit then arises in accordance with them. As for what is performed in the human realm, it is the [deeds] of the heavenly realm.
If one performs the karma of a deva, the spirit follows it and is born in the heavens;

if one performs the karma of an asura, the spirit follows it and is born among the asuras; if one performs the karma of the three evil realms, the spirit follows it and is born in those three evil realms.
Thus, in this cycle through the six destinies, there is no time of escape. Furthermore, as for this spirit, from beginningless time...
Transmigrating into a womb or changing one's shell, the spirit cannot remain long in a single place. Why is this so?
It is because the karma I have created will not be exhausted until a long time has passed. Thus, the spirit dwells within this karma; when the karma is exhausted, the physical form perishes.
Once the form has perished, the spirit has no place to dwell and must proceed according to the karma I have created in this present life.
For example, when a person builds a house, they must dwell within it; when a person prepares food, they must enjoy its flavor.
Thus, when one creates such karma, one must inevitably receive such retribution; this is the natural law.
Therefore, how can I not be cautious regarding what I do in this present life?
The Sūtra says: "The Great King of Physicians can cure all diseases, yet he cannot cure one whose life has reached its end;
the Buddha can deliver all sentient beings, yet he cannot deliver those who lack faith. Faith is but a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*).

If, during one's lifetime, the mind intends for the body to go, the body follows that intention to go; if the mind intends for the body to stay, the body follows that intention to stay—such is the nature of this body.

Even if one constantly maintains mindfulness while still having thoughts of desire to depart and the body remains bound by attachments, at the time of the body’s dissolution there will be but a single thought;
once that single thought reaches its destination, there is nowhere it cannot go.

Therefore, if a single thought is directed toward the Pure Land, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land—how much more so when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas personally welcome and lead people to rebirth there?
Zhiguizi asked Master Shandao: "I have received your instructions on the method of nianfo (buddha-recitation), yet I fear that at the moment of death my consciousness will become distracted.
I further worry that others may disturb my right mindfulness, causing me to lose the pure cause.
The Master said: "Excellent question! For all people at the end of life, one must simply not be afraid of death; one should constantly reflect upon this body."
When one is beset by much suffering, if one can attain equanimity (*upekṣā*) and be reborn in a Pure Land to experience immeasurable bliss, this is truly a matter of fulfilling one's wishes;
it is like casting off tattered rags to exchange them for precious garments. One should not harbor any lingering attachment to those tattered rags.

Rather, when encountering illness, one should contemplate impermanence (*anityatā*) and wait single-mindedly for death, instructing one’s family members and those who come to inquire after one’s health or provide medical care.
When such a person comes before me, you must not engage in idle or trivial conversation;
nor should you offer soft words of consolation, prayers for their well-being, or blessings, as these are all like empty flowers and of no benefit.

If they are gravely ill and approaching death, their relatives must not weep, wail, lament, or express grief, which would only disturb and confuse their minds. Instead, you should all chant the Buddha’s name together to assist them.
When it comes to the funeral rites for one who has attained rebirth in the Pure Land, it is not too late to weep once a long period has passed after their breath has ceased.

If one knows that death is a departure, being able to refrain from weeping is even more indicative of profound understanding. Furthermore, when reborn in the Pure Land, one abandons suffering and attains bliss;

therefore, one must carefully avoid wailing and crying, as these may disturb the mind of the deceased. Moreover, I have frequently observed that people in the world practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) during their ordinary lives.

When one offers praise and makes vows to seek rebirth in the Western Paradise, yet upon falling ill, one again fears death and says nothing of the matter of rebirth—waiting until the breath has ceased and life is spent, and consciousness has entered the realm of darkness, before finally reciting the ten recitations while ringing the bell—is this not like closing the gate after the thief has fled?
Of what benefit is it? The matter of birth and death is great; one must exert effort for oneself.
If you have only just attained this and allow even a single thought to stray, you will suffer for kalpas on end; who can take your place? Think on this! Think on this!
The Patriarch Cizhao’s *Ten Gates of Admonition for the Pure Land* states: "A practitioner of nianfo facing death must be careful regarding the three doubts and three barriers.
First, the doubt: 'I have committed heavy karma since birth, while my practice has been shallow for only a few days; I fear I shall not [attain rebirth].'"

There are three doubts regarding rebirth: first, the doubt that one has come into this life owing a debt to others or harbors unfulfilled aspirations, or that greed, anger, and delusion have not yet ceased, and thus fears one may not attain birth;
second, the doubt that although one recites the name of Amitābha, one fears the Buddha will not come to welcome and guide one at the moment of death;
third, the doubt that due to these three uncertainties, they become obstacles that cause one to lose right mindfulness and fail to attain rebirth.
For those who practice *nien-fo* for the sake of rebirth in the Pure Land, it is essential to believe the Buddha’s words with utmost sincerity and not give rise to doubt. Regarding the "Three Gates":
although ordinary beings possess faith and practice *nien-fo*, because their karmic obstacles from past lives are heavy, they ought to fall into hell;

yet at the moment of death, they cannot avoid the suffering of illness. If, through this suffering of illness, they attain realization and repentance, their body and mind will certainly be born in the Pure Land. This is solely because...
Ignorant people do not understand this matter, yet they say, "I am now reciting the Buddha's name," even while suffering from illness;

Second, although one may observe the precepts and recite the Buddha's name, because they habitually speak of the Pure Land with their mouths while their hearts remain attached to Saṃsāra, they encounter illness at the time of death.
Fearing death and craving life, they believe in and accept the calls of children to spirits and ghosts; they burn money and paper and slaughter living beings.
Because their minds are thus perverse and lack the protection of the Buddhas, they fall into the three miserable realms—this is the second barrier.
Third, at the moment of death, they remain bound to their wealth and possessions and harbor deep attachment to their kin; unable to let go, they look back toward their households and fall.
Within the realm of hungry ghosts, one may become a stingy dog or take the form of a snake to guard one's household as if it were still one's own day;

It is precisely because of the sufferings of saṃsāra that I am now willing to recite the Buddha’s name and cultivate practice;
I vow to abandon this Saha world and aspire to be born in the Pure Land. I now speak directly to you, my worthy friend: you must see those people in this world.
Who does not love sensual desire? Who does not enjoy wine and meat? Who does not covet fame and profit? Who does not wish for wealth and honor?

If one now attempts to forcibly suppress them to establish an immediate state of empty stillness, then movement will return to that stillness, and stillness will only cause movement to intensify further. Even if coarse thoughts are temporarily stilled, subtle thoughts will still persist."

One might then say that such correspondence is erroneous and not a minor matter; since one dwells in the realm of ordinary beings, one has not yet been able to sever discursive thought or forget external conditions.

Why not, then, take those very conditions and thoughts as the basis for cultivation? Therefore, use mindfulness to strike back at every moment of thought, replacing hundreds of thousands of millions of miscellaneous thoughts with the name of a single Buddha.
Just as delusion arises from the True and waves follow the water, so too is every thought [the Buddha].
Since emptiness is the fundamental essence and awakening (bodhi) is not attained separately outside of thought, it is said that "the myriad dharmas are illusory and there is only the one mind";
by awakening to one's own mind, everything encountered is bodhi.

Furthermore, it is said that if one practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) alone, the *skandha-māras* may arise, as is explained in great detail in various sūtras and śāstras such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* and the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.

However, for those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, because of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and the power of his original vows, there will certainly be no demonic activities within his great radiance.
Nevertheless, if one has deep-seated karmic obstructions from past lives or fails to apply the mind skillfully, it is still possible for demons to arise; this is truly not to be taken lightly.
One must certainly identify in advance what is taught in the sūtras and śāstras: when a practitioner sees the Buddha, there are two ways to discern this.
First, that which does not accord with the sūtras is the work of Māra; second, that which does not accord with one's original practice is the work of Māra.
The reason for this is that for a person who practices meditation alone, the cause originally cultivated consists solely of mind without external objects.
As for the appearance of Buddhas externally, we set all such instances aside as irrelevant because the result does not accord with the cause;

however, for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they recollect the Buddha throughout their lives and see the Buddha at the moment of death—since cause and effect thus correspond, how can one doubt that this is the work of a demon?

Someone asked: "The teaching of the Pure Land is merely a symbolic expression of the Dharma. A person of wisdom should directly awaken to the Zen school; why then do you now only praise and speak of the Pure Land?

Will this not lead to attachment to phenomenal forms and a failure to understand the nature of principle? I replied: "The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of expedient means.
If one understands this meaning, then Zen and the Pure Land are different paths that lead to the same destination. This is what you have asked about.
Doubts were instantly dispelled. Among the ancients, there have been countless instances of mutual elucidation on this point.
Master Zhongfeng said, "For Chan practitioners, there is Pure Land Chan; for Pure Land, there is Chan-Pure Land. Those who practice must value entering deeply into one gate.
These few words remain an unchanging definitive doctrine for ten thousand generations. Therefore, the Great Power...

When a Bodhisattva attains the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), it is said that they enter the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha;
when Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the inconceivable liberation of the *Avataṃsaka*, he says, "May I, at the end of my life, be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
These two great beings—one attending the Teacher of the Sahā world and one attending the Guide of the Sukhāvatī—should each be established separately.
To harmonize and integrate these gateways such that they are perfectly interfused and mutually unimpeded is something everyone has commonly heard and knows well;
how could one still cling to biased views? Furthermore, when you say that the Pure Land represents a dharma, is it not because the pure mind itself is the Pure Land?
If so, would you then also claim that a virtuous mind is itself heaven?
How could there be further Yama or Trāyastriṃśa heavens? The evil mind itself is hell; how could there be further swords, blades, or boiling cauldrons?
The deluded mind itself is the animal realm; how could there be further beings with fur and horns?

Furthermore, you delight in discussing the nature of reality while detesting the explanation of conventional phenomena; this is entirely because you wish to manifest yourself as a high monk and fear others.

If you say that I am not conversant with the principles of nature (xingli), then if one truly possesses a penetrating understanding of the principle, one will know that there is no principle apart from phenomena and no nature apart from appearances;
they are fundamentally interpenetrating. Why, then, must one insist on abandoning phenomena to seek principle, or leaving this earth to find the mind?

Furthermore, you divide the lands into four types, yet you claim there is only the land of serene light (jiguang zhen tu) and that there are no other lands such as the land of true reward and adornment (shibao zhuangyan tu).

If you merely speak of the single flavor of signlessness to seek loftiness and subtlety, then the claim that "the mind is the pure land" is something that newly initiated students can understand after studying two or three volumes of sutras and treatises; what difficulty is there in speaking such words?
Furthermore, since you maintain that the mind is pure and thus the land is pure, and that purity exists everywhere, I ask you this: would you be willing to dwell right within a latrine?
Will you stop? Will you consent to share a trough for drinking and eating with dogs, pigs, oxen, and horses? Will you consent to enter burial mounds and tombs to sleep alongside stinking corpses?
Will you consent to wash, massage, feed, and nurse those afflicted by kāmalā, pus, blood, excrement, urine, and various foul diseases, for many months and years?
Regarding these several matters, will you remain joyful and at ease? Briefly [put it this way].
I do not mind your claim that high mountains and level plains are all the Western Land;

however, if you outwardly endure such claims while inwardly harboring doubt and resentment, then the distinction between pure and impure realms remains unemptied and feelings of hatred and attachment still persist.

To then open your mouth and boastfully discourse upon the transcendent states of the Great Sage, while denying the existence of Buddha-lands and holding the practice of rebirth in contempt—this may indeed be called...
To deceive Heaven and delude men while taking pleasure in one's own bitterness—how bitter, how bitter!

Furthermore, if you possess great power and a great vow, willing to emerge and submerge yourself again and again within the ocean of birth and death to practice the bodhisattva path without fear or timidity, then rebirth in the Pure Land would not be forced upon you by me.
However, if you harbor concerns that the winds of the environment in this land will become turbulent and act as your master, [then you must seek the Pure Land].
One must not harbor the worry that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter and thus there is no way to practice;

nor should one worry that the power of patience is not yet firm and thus cannot deliver sentient beings from the perilous places of the triple world; nor should one worry that this retribution-body will end but one has not yet permanently severed birth and death to avoid future existence;
nor should one worry that since future existence still lies ahead, the path after casting off this body and before receiving the next is vast and desolate, with no known destination.
To depart now and abandon the Pure Land so as not to be reborn there is a fault that is no small matter. This Dharma-gate of the Pure Land appears shallow yet is profound;

it appears near yet is distant; it appears difficult yet is easy; it appears easy yet is difficult. You shall know this for yourself in the future, but for now, believe it with earnest conviction and quickly be diligent in your speech.
Do not indulge your verbal karma to bring calamity upon yourself or others, lest you bequeath the retribution of suffering to the measureless eons.
This is the ultimate point.
Zen Master Gekkei said: "The *ming-ling* (the caterpillar) does not originally possess wings; the *kuei-lo* (the wasp) buries it and chants incantations over it.

Through these ceaseless incantations, the *ming-ling* transforms according to the sound, and wings and feathers grow upon it. Although these words concern a small matter, they can serve as a profound analogy.

It is illustrated by the fact that all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are sustained by the conceptual framework of sentient beings; their defiled and pure karmic fruits transform according to their perceptions.
When one perceives the earth as blue, the entire great earth becomes blue. When the mind conceives of the Buddha, would the great earth not then be the Buddha?
In the *Western Pure Land Synthesis* (*Xi-fang-he-lun*), Layman Yuan states: "There was a mad monk who prided himself on his realization.
I asked him, 'Do you believe that you have left the household life? Do you believe that your body is in Chang'an? The monk was startled and said, 'How could I not believe it?
I replied, 'In your dreams, or perhaps when dreaming of the time before you left the household life, do you ever see your parents and brothers? Or when you were a child...'"
"When you were playing as a child, did you know at that time that you were staying in someone else's house? The monk said, "I did not know.

I said, "In discussing your conviction in leaving home to become a monk and your subsequent journeying as a pilgrim, you must have been extremely clear and penetrating. Your realization of the Way was surely no less than this;
yet, as soon as you reached your pillow, you returned from being a monk to being a layman, changed 'guest' back to 'home,' and did not even know it yourself."
"How much less can one who relies on a mere fragment of insight during the long night of birth and death ensure that they will not fall into error?
At these words, the monk was struck with awe.
The *Jingtu jue* states: "That which is called 'Buddha-recitation' (nianfo) is not the recitation of the mouth, but rather the recitation of the mind."
That which the mind contemplates is where the imagination focuses, where the will inclines, where affection concentrates, and where emotion is bound;
it is the ultimate limit of thought and that which must be attained through deliberation—this can be seen by observing the world of men.
When there are those in the world who take beauty as their primary concern, every thought is fixed solely upon beauty, and apart from beauty, all other things [are disregarded].

One does not give it one's heart-mind; rather, those who take the management of livelihood as their heart-mind will, in every thought-moment, produce wealth, and apart from wealth, nothing else enters their hearts.
Although such people never actually recite these things with their mouths all day long, they anticipate them and look toward them with longing, ceasing not day or night;
thus, few fail to realize what they have envisioned, for that which is held in the heart-mind is firm.
Although one’s thoughts may occasionally be interspersed with other matters, they ultimately cannot displace one’s right mindfulness;
thus, the practitioner of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) may be known. For the human mind is most urgent in its attachments:
like water that must flow to the sea, like fire that must blaze upward, like a sharp blade that must wound, and like a poisonous drug that must kill—such thoughts do not pass away in vain.
The Buddha’s mindfulness is also like this: even if one does not bring a single name of the Buddha to mind all day long, one is nonetheless recollecting the Buddha throughout that entire day.

Conversely, if one is wavering between faith and doubt, uncertain whether the Western Land truly exists or not, then even if one recites the Buddha’s name as a daily practice, taking a thousand recitations as a ritual rule, it will be nothing more than a labor in vain.
The Three Great Sages Manifest Themselves to Exhort People to Cultivate Pure Karma:
During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, Shi Huiri of Wangji Temple in Luoyang received ordination.

Having personally witnessed the Tripitaka Master Yijing’s journey to India, he conceived a deep admiration and vowed to travel to the Western Regions. He first embarked on a ship to cross the sea, and after three years had passed...
He then traveled to India to seek out Sanskrit manuscripts and visit virtuous spiritual friends, journeying alone and on foot through snow-capped mountains and foreign lands, reaching every place.
Having endured many hardships and becoming deeply weary of Jambudvīpa, he sighed and said: "In which kingdom or direction is there joy without suffering?
What dharma or what practice can lead one swiftly to see the Buddha? He questioned all the Tripitaka masters throughout India, and they all...

Having recited the *Praise of the Pure Land* (*Sukhāvatīvyūha*) over a thousand times daily and received it with reverence upon hearing it, he gradually traveled to the northern Indian region of Gandhāra.
To the northeast of the royal city, there was a great mountain where a statue of Avalokiteśvara resided.
He prayed before it day after day for seven days, vowing to end his life through fasting as his limit. On the night of the seventh day, Avalokiteśvara appeared in the air in a body of purple-gold.

The deity of form extended his right hand, stroked the crown of the Sun’s head, and said: "If you are to transmit the Dharma for the benefit of yourself and others, there is only the Western Land of Amitābha.
You must exhort people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, recite the sutras, and dedicate their merit toward rebirth there.

Once you have reached that land and seen the Buddha and myself, you shall naturally know that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land surpasses all other practices. Having spoken, he suddenly vanished, and the Sun was cut off.

Already exhausted from his travels, he was invigorated upon hearing this news. When he reached the mountain pass and turned eastward to return home, he calculated that he had traveled through more than seventy kingdoms over a total of eighteen years.
It was not until the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era that he finally arrived in Chang’an, where he presented the Emperor with the true likeness of the Buddha and Sanskrit manuscripts;
the Emperor conferred upon him the title "Tripiṭaka Master Wang Fashi of Compassion."

Furthermore, in the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, the Great Master Fazhao resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou, where he practiced with unremitting diligence, making the exhortation of others to practice *nianfo* his primary concern.
One day, within his alms bowl during two servings of morning gruel, the magnificent scenery of Mount Wutai appeared;
within that vision, there was further a temple with a golden plaque inscribed: "The Great Sage’s Bamboo Grove Temple."
Thereupon, harboring a heart of yearning and reverence, he set out on the thirteenth day of the eighth month in the fourth year with the desire to pay homage at Mount Wutai.
He arrived at Wutai County on the sixteenth day of the fourth month in the fifth year; from afar, he saw several streaks of white light to the south of Foguang Temple.
On the sixth day, he reached Foguang Temple. That night, during the fourth watch, he saw a beam of light descend from the northern mountain, shining and illuminating everything.
Hurrying into the inner chamber, he asked the assembly, "What auspicious sign is this? A monk replied, "This is the inconceivable light of the Great Sage;

it constantly perceives those with whom it has a karmic connection and shines upon them. Having heard this, he immediately assumed a dignified demeanor and followed the light to a place fifty *li* northeast of the monastery.
Indeed, there was a mountain; at its foot lay a stream, and to the north of the stream stood a stone gate, where two youths dressed in green were seen.
A youth of about eight or nine years of age, with a handsome and upright countenance, stood at the gate; one was named Sudhana and the other Nanda.
Seeing each other, they rejoiced, exchanged greetings, and performed salutations. They were led through the gate and traveled north for five or six *li*, where they saw a golden gate-tower.
Upon reaching the gate, they found it was a monastery, and upon the golden plaque before the temple, the name "Great Sage Zhulin Monastery" was inscribed.
Just as he had seen within the bowl, the area was approximately twenty *li* in circumference; one hundred and twenty monasteries were all adorned with jeweled stupas.
The ground was made entirely of pure gold, and flowing channels and flowering trees filled its interior.
Light entered the temple and reached the lecture hall, where he saw Mañjuśrī in the west and Samantabhadra in the east, each seated upon a lion throne, preaching the Dharma.
The sound of the Dharma was clearly audible. To the left and right of Mañjuśrī were more than ten thousand bodhisattvas, and Samantabhadra was likewise surrounded by countless bodhisattvas.
Their radiance reached the two bodhisattvas, who paid homage and asked: "In this final age, ordinary beings are far removed from the sages;
their spiritual teachers have grown inferior, and their defilements and obscurations are even deeper. The Buddha-Dharma is vast and profound; we do not know how to practice it."
“Which dharma-gate is the most swift and essential? Mañjuśrī replied, “Now is the very time for you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Among all gates of cultivation, none surpasses mindfulness of the Buddha. Why is this? Because in past kalpas, it was through mindfulness of the Buddha that I attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, the Dharma of all Buddhas and the Prajñāpāramitā are profoundly deep.”

"Since everything from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) up to the Buddhas arises from the mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), you should know that the mindfulness of the Buddha is the sovereign of all dharmas.
You must practice the mindfulness of the Unsurpassed Dharma-King without ceasing, so that it may illuminate [all things]. Again he asked, "How should one practice this mindfulness?
Mañjuśrī replied, "To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha. The power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable; you..."
"Maintain mindfulness so that it remains uninterrupted; after the end of this life, you will certainly be reborn there and never fall back.
Having spoken these words, the two Great Sages each extended their golden hands and stroked Prajñābhāsa’s head, bestowing upon him the prediction of enlightenment.
Upon hearing this, Prajñābhāsa was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated himself in gratitude and withdrew.

Testimonies of Rebirth through Reciting the Sutra (as seen in the *Lianchi Shuchao*):
Those who recite this sutra will have their tongues remain intact at death; when celestial music welcomes them to the West, they shall then resolve their karmic grudges and attain rebirth.

Sitting and passing away at the end of the scroll is like entering meditative concentration; at the end, one beholds the white lotus and the silver terrace being transformed into the golden terrace, and the coarse music being replaced by the subtle music.
Regarding those whose tongue-roots do not decay, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there was a bhikṣu who recited the *Amitābha-sūtra*; when his life was about to end—
He said to his disciples, "Amitābha Buddha has come with the great assembly to welcome me.
Later, after being cremated, his tongue remained unburnt and its color was naturally as it had been; heavenly music welcomed him from the west. This occurred during the Song and Tang dynasties.
A man who had recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* one hundred thousand times once told his family members, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and having said this, he passed away.
During his funeral rites, that night a virtuous practitioner was traveling on the road when he dreamed of Mount Daowei.

There, he saw wondrous lights and banners of flowers from the West drifting about, and music resounded clearly in the air. A voice from the sky proclaimed: "Tang Shi-liang has already been born in the Pure Land;
those who have resolved their grudges and attained rebirth include Feng Min, a commoner of Shangyu, Song, who in his youth pursued hunting and once encountered a giant serpent which he captured."
When he was about to go and strike it, the snake was at the foot of a rock, intending to devour a yellow calf; Min pushed the rock down upon it until it died.
Although the snake repeatedly caused him trouble, Min practiced repentance and recited the Buddha’s name for years, so the snake could not harm him.
One day, he invited his fellow practitioners to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*; with palms joined, he passed away while still seated before the session had ended.

The Dharma Master Zhixian of the Jin dynasty was titled Zhenjiao; he resided at Bailian Temple for thirteen years, reciting the name of Amitābha ten times while facing west throughout the twelve periods of the day without ceasing even for a moment.
One night, suffering from a slight illness, he instructed the practitioners of the Guantang Hall to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Before the scroll was finished, he passed away sitting upright, as serene as one entering meditative absorption. The monk Chuchen of the Song dynasty cultivated the Pure Land with great diligence.
One evening, Tu finished reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra* and, praising the Pure Land, addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have been born in the Pure Land through non-arising, as if entering a state of meditative concentration. She then passed away suddenly; those who witnessed her end beheld a white lotus.

This was the Lady Zhong of Jiahe Prefecture during the Song dynasty, who recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* ten times daily and never ceased the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha. One day, she spoke to her [disciples].
The Master said: "I saw countless white lotuses and a multitude of sages welcoming me; I then sat upright, straightened my body, and passed away.
As for the Silver Terrace and Golden Terrace, these were Chan Master Huaiyu of Taizhou. He wore plain clothes, ate but one meal a day, and remained constantly seated without lying down.
He was diligent in the recitation of the Buddha’s name and chanted the *Amitābha Sūtra* three hundred thousand times. One day, he beheld the sages of the Western Paradise.
A multitude as numerous as the sands of the Ganges raised a silver platform together and entered through the window.

Fayingyu said, "Throughout my life I have practiced with diligence, vowing to attain a golden platform; why have I obtained this silver platform? Thereupon, she vanished. Fayingyu was moved by deep gratitude and redoubled her diligent practice.
After twenty-one days, she saw Buddhas filling the sky and said to her disciples, "The golden platform has come to welcome me."
"I have been born in the Pure Land. Having spoken this verse, he passed away with a smile on his face.
County Governor Du Gong was struck by this marvel and composed a poem in praise of him, containing the line: "The branches bend low only to hang upon the Golden Terrace.

As for the "Coarse Pleasures and Subtle Pleasures," they refer to Chan Master Yuan Zihuā, who in the ninth year of the Dali era recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* six times at Guanyin Temple in Runzhou.
Yue suddenly fell ill; one night, he smelled a fragrance and heard the sound of music, as a voice from the air announced: "Coarse pleasures have already passed;

subtle pleasures follow in succession. You shall be reborn in the Pure Land. After some time, he passed away while reciting the Buddha's name, and a wondrous fragrance did not dissipate for several days.
Furthermore, as for transcribing [the scriptures], their transformative influence reaches the common people; as for expounding them, auspicious signs such as white cranes appear.

Regarding transcription, the Tang dynasty Master Shandao obtained offerings and used them to transcribe one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, encouraging others to receive and uphold it;
there were also those who recited it up to one hundred thousand times or even five hundred thousand times.

Monastics and laypeople alike looked up to him with such profound devotion that there were countless instances of those who offered themselves by burning their bodies as an act of worship and attained the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation.

Among his lecturers was Shen Sanlang of the Song dynasty, who in his later years turned his heart toward the recitation of the Buddha’s name. When he fell ill, he requested a monk to preach the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*;
he changed his robes and passed away while sitting with his knees drawn up, wishing to rise, though his two sons restrained him out of deference to the formal teachings of the Confucian tradition.
When they were about to move his coffin from the easy-to-shift position to the difficult-to-drag one, he straightened his legs.

As they were about to enter him for cremation, he suddenly raised his head, pushed aside the shrouds, and sat up with a startle. The entire family was greatly alarmed; his two sons hurried forward to support and protect him, but he struck them with his elbows and knees.
His sons said, "We are merely helping our father to sit through his passing. He finally passed away while sitting. During the cremation, twenty-nine white cranes appeared.
A single bird flew and cried out above the clouds for a long time before departing to the west.
As for manifesting such responses in the present, one may behold them from afar upon the precious ground; as for attaining rebirth through focused practice, Nirvana is beyond compare.
Such manifestations have been witnessed repeatedly throughout the ages.

Regarding those who gazed from afar at the Jewel Ground: when Chan Master Tang Daxing first practiced the Samantabhadra Repentance, he subsequently entered the Tripitaka and took up a fascicle at random, obtaining the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
He recited it day and night until the twenty-first day, at which time he beheld the Buddha and the two Great Beings appearing before him upon the ground of lapis lazuli.
When Emperor Xizong heard of these events, he issued an imperial decree for the Master to enter the inner court and bestowed [honors] upon him.
The Bodhisattva named Constant Diligence (Chang Jingjin) later appeared on the lapis lazuli ground;
it was seen that he passed away on that very day, and for ten days a rare fragrance remained while his physical body did not decay—a state of nirvana beyond comparison.

During the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, when the Dharma Master Daozhen was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he stayed at Mount Lu. Admiring Master Huiyuan’s pure practices, while sitting in meditation, he suddenly saw [a vision] upon the sea.
Several hundred people were traveling forward in a precious boat, and the Master asked them where they were going. They replied, "We are going to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

When he asked if he might be allowed to join them, they answered, "Although you, Dharma Master, are skilled in lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—which is itself most inconceivable—you have not yet recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*;
how can you go with us? The Master thereupon ceased his lectures, focused his mind on the Buddha, and began to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

As he was nearing the completion of twenty thousand recitations of the sutra, during the fourth watch of the night four weeks prior to his passing, he saw a silver platform from the west arrive in the air, as bright as the midday sun.
A voice proclaimed, "Dharma Master, you shall ascend this platform to be reborn in the Pure Land.
At that time, the assembly all heard celestial music and extraordinary fragrances; for several days, the fragrance did not dissipate. That night, the monks of Fengding Temple [perceived these signs].
From afar he saw dozens of torches at the mouth of the valley, their bright flames blazing through the night; it was only on the following day that he learned the Master had passed away.
As recorded above, these instances of cultivating causes and realizing fruits, where this response arises from that stimulus, have appeared one after another in layers;
from ancient times to the present, they are too numerous to be easily enumerated.
Regarding rebirth through the holding of the Name:
for those who hold the Name, perhaps a single thought-moment sends forth a ray of light, or a single utterance brings forth a Buddha;

perhaps the resonance fills the forests and valleys, or the sound penetrates the imperial palace; perhaps one maintains mindfulness throughout the six periods of the day and night, such that the primary and secondary marks fill the void, or ten...

The characters [of the name] mark the mind, through which sages and worthies entered the assembly; continuing down to the present illustrious era, there have been successive streams of renowned practitioners.

This precisely clarifies the practice of upholding the Name. Among the many virtuous ones of the Pure Land school, I shall not record them at length, but will briefly cite one or two who were so radiant as to be witnessed by the ears and eyes of the world, to serve as an exhortation.
As for Feiguang (Flaming Light), he was the Tang dynasty’s Shandao Da... [text ends].
When a master asked him, "Can one attain birth in the Pure Land through the recitation of the Buddha's name? he replied, "As you have recited, so shall your wish be fulfilled.
Thereupon, Dao led [the Emperor] to personally recite the name of Amitābha Buddha once; then a ray of light issued from his mouth.
When he recited ten times up to a hundred times, the same occurred each time, and the radiance filled the chamber. When the Emperor heard of this matter, he issued an imperial decree.
The place where he resided was Guangming Temple; later, he ascended to the top of a willow tree and passed away while sitting upright.
As for the manifestation of Buddhas, Dharma Master Shaokang established a Pure Land practice hall at Mount Niaolong and exhorted people to recite the Buddha’s name.
When the assembly saw the Master recite the name once, a Buddha emerged from his mouth; when he recited it ten times, ten Buddhas emerged in succession, appearing like a string of pearls.
On the day of his death, several extraordinary rays of light spiraled from his mouth, and he passed away suddenly;

this was the Tang dynasty Chan Master Dàochuó, who during his lifetime lectured on the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* nearly two hundred times for the assembly, with each person counting their beads and reciting the Buddha’s name, so that at times the sound spread through the forests and valleys as the session dispersed.
This was the Tang dynasty Fǎzhào, whose voice reached far and wide.
In Bingzhou, during the fifth assembly of the Nianfo (Buddha-recitation) practice, Emperor Daizong heard the sound of recitation within the palace.

He dispatched an envoy to search for its source and found the Master; impressed by the flourishing of his proselytizing, the Emperor then summoned him to the palace. There, the palace ladies also engaged in the five assemblies of recitation, leading to the Master being titled the "Dharma Master of the Five Assemblies.
As for the six periods [of daily recitation], they were established by Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty while he resided at Mount Lu.

Having practiced mindfulness of the Buddha with a purified mind and focused attention during the six periods of the day using a lotus-flower water clock, nineteen years later, on the evening of the final day of the seventh month, while at the Prajñā Terrace, he arose from meditative concentration and beheld Amitābha Buddha, whose body filled the entirety of space.
Within his circular halo were immeasurable transformation Buddhas and a multitude of Bodhisattvas. From the flowing radiance, the wondrous Dharma was proclaimed. The Buddha—
He said, "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you; seven days from now, you shall be born in my land.

When the appointed time arrived, he passed away while sitting upright. As for the ten characters [of the inscription], they refer to Chan Master Zongze of Changlu in the Song dynasty, who had deeply realized the principles of Chan and was thoroughly versed in both the school (Chan) and the teachings (Scriptures).
Following the regulations of Mount Lu, he established the "Lotus Assembly," the ritual method of which was as follows:

Every day he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha a thousand or ten thousand times; for each thousand recitations, he made a mark with a cross at the end of the day. One night, he dreamed of a man wearing a black cap and white robes, whose appearance was refined and beautiful. The man said to Zhe, "I wish to enter your assembly for Amitābha; I beg you to write down my name. Zhe asked the man what his name was, and he replied, "Puhui.
